result.recommendation: The mutex is only process-local, so with 4-12 Kubernetes replicas concurrent requests for the same coupon can enter the critical section independently and both pass the redeemedAt check. Replace it with an atomic database claim (conditional update or transaction) backed by a coupon redemption state and payment idempotency/reconciliation; keep the concurrency test, but run it across multiple application processes or replicas.
critical_assumptions: All redemption requests are routed through the same Node.js process, which is false for the stated HPA deployment unless the Service or traffic policy guarantees it.
The mutex remains held until the coupon update completes, including successful charge and database update.
The payment provider can safely handle retries, including requests whose prior result is unknown.
Coupon code and order association have database-enforced uniqueness.
Coupon state can represent pending or reserved redemption, not only redeemedAt.
material_risks: Two replicas can both read an unredeemed coupon, both charge orders, and both update the coupon.
A process crash or pod termination after charging but before update leaves an externally paid order with a redeemable coupon.
A charge timeout may trigger a retry that charges again unless the payment request is idempotent.
The in-memory Map provides no correctness across restarts, pod eviction, or multiple Node.js workers.
A test using two concurrent calls in one process can pass while the production multi-replica race remains.
result.better_alternative: Use an atomic Postgres claim such as updateMany({ where: { code, status: "AVAILABLE", redeemedAt: null }, data: { status: "PENDING", orderId, reservedAt } }) and require exactly one affected row. Charge through a provider idempotency key derived from the order, then transition to REDEEMED; retries and reconciliation must first inspect the existing pending redemption and provider status. Add a unique constraint and expiration/recovery handling for abandoned reservations.

falsification_probe.description: Run two redemption requests for the same unused coupon simultaneously through separate application processes or two Kubernetes replicas, using distinct orders, and record charge and database results.

result.recommendation: The in-process mutex cannot serialize requests across the 4–12 replicas, so concurrent retries routed to different pods can both redeem the coupon. Use a Postgres-backed atomic state transition or distributed lock, ideally with a unique redemption record and idempotent order charging; explicitly define compensation or retry behavior if charging fails after the coupon is claimed.
critical_assumptions: All redemption requests for a coupon may reach different application replicas.
Postgres is shared by every replica and is the authoritative consistency boundary.
A coupon may have only one successful redemption across the entire service.
Payment charging can be made idempotent or reconciled with the coupon state transition.

The concurrency test can pass in one Node process while masking the production multi-replica failure.
Claiming before charging can consume the coupon when charging fails unless compensation or a pending state exists.
Holding a database transaction or lock across payment I/O may violate the checkout p99 target.
result.better_alternative: Replace the process-local mutex with a database-level compare-and-set or transaction. For example, atomically transition an eligible coupon to a unique pending redemption using `UPDATE ... WHERE redeemed_at IS NULL AND status = 'AVAILABLE'`; persist a unique order/redemption identifier, then make charging idempotent and finalize or compensate pending claims. A unique redemption ledger or constraint provides an additional correctness barrier.

falsification_probe.description: In a test environment, deploy at least two replicas and send simultaneous same-code redemption requests with connections explicitly routed to different pods; repeat enough times to cover the observed 50–300 ms overlap.

result.recommendation: Replace the process-local mutex with a durable, atomic Postgres reservation using a conditional status update and a unique coupon redemption constraint. Reserve using a stable order/idempotency key before charging, then finalize or reconcile by order ID; do not hold a database lock during payment I/O.
critical_assumptions: All redemption requests for a coupon are routed to the same process instance.
No competing application instance, pod, or horizontally scaled replica exists.
Processes cannot restart or crash between reading and updating the coupon.

The solution does not define safe behavior for payment timeouts, retries, failures, or abandoned reservations.
The test only validates one process and therefore provides no evidence of cross-replica correctness.

Finalize or reconcile reservations by stable order ID.

falsification_probe.description: Start two independent application instances against the same database and issue simultaneous redemption requests for the same coupon code, one to each instance.

result.recommendation: An in-process mutex cannot serialize the 4-12 Kubernetes replicas, so concurrent requests routed to different pods can still both pass the check and redeem the coupon. Replace it with a Postgres-backed atomic redemption claim or unique redemption record, and make charging/retry handling idempotent so a client retry cannot create a second order charge.
critical_assumptions: All redemption requests for a coupon are routed to the same process, which is false with multiple replicas.
The service is not horizontally scaled or restarted during the redemption window.
The charge operation can be safely retried or reconciled using an idempotency key.

result.better_alternative: Use a durable Postgres operation: atomically claim the coupon with an UPDATE ... WHERE redeemedAt IS NULL and a unique redemption identifier, or insert into a redemptions table with UNIQUE(coupon_id). Persist an order/payment idempotency key and state transitions so retries return the existing result; handle charge failure with an explicit recoverable state and reconciliation. Add a test that sends concurrent requests through separate service instances or directly validates the atomic database operation.

falsification_probe.description: Run two concurrent redeem requests for one coupon while forcing them to different pods, for example by scaling the Deployment to at least two replicas and targeting separate pod IPs through separate test clients.

result.recommendation: Replace the in-process mutex with a database-enforced available/pending state machine and pass a stable idempotency key to chargeOrder. Atomically claim a coupon with a conditional update; only the request that changes state may charge, and retries must return the existing redemption result rather than charge again. Add a cross-process integration test, not only an in-memory concurrent-call test.
critical_assumptions: All redemption requests can be coordinated through the same Postgres database.
The in-process mutex would be shared by every request, which is false with four to twelve Deployment replicas.
The existing single-process test is representative of the client retry path.
chargeOrder can be coordinated by serializing execution, despite being an external side effect.
Postgres uniqueness or conditional updates can enforce one successful claimant.
material_risks: Concurrent requests routed to different pods can both observe an unused coupon and both charge, continuing the financial loss.
A process crash after charging but before setting redeemedAt permanently permits another redemption.
A client retry after an ambiguous two-second timeout can charge twice even if the original process completed.
The Map and cleanup logic can leak mutex entries or leave incorrect state under exceptional concurrency.
The proposed test passes in one process while providing no protection for the actual production topology.

SET status='pending', redemption_id=?, order_id=? WHERE code=? AND status='available'. Execute the idempotent charge under that claim, finalize it conditionally, and have retries look up and resume or return the existing result. This coordinates all pods, makes ownership durable, and addresses post-charge timeout retries; rollout should be expedited with the smallest safe schema and service changes this week.

falsification_probe.description: Run two concurrent redemption requests for one fresh coupon through two different pod instances, with the first call delayed between the read and charge, and inspect coupon state plus charge-provider idempotency records.

result.recommendation: Do not use a process-local mutex when every deployment has multiple replicas; requests for the same coupon can reach different processes and both pass the unlocked check. Enforce the invariant in Postgres with an atomic conditional claim or a unique redemption record, then handle payment idempotency and ambiguous client retries explicitly.
critical_assumptions: All requests for a coupon necessarily reach the same Node.js process, which is contradicted by the Deployment HPA and round-robin Service.
A new request cannot enter between check and update, including after lock cleanup or process termination.
chargeOrder and the subsequent coupon update are atomic or recoverable as one business operation.
A successful coupon update cannot be lost after money has been charged.
The client retry is the only source of duplicate attempts, rather than concurrent requests already in flight.
material_risks: Two requests routed to different pods can both observe redeemedAt as null and both redeem the coupon, preserving the reported loss mechanism.
A process crash after charging but before setting redeemedAt leaves a paid order with an apparently reusable coupon.
Map cleanup can create overlapping mutexes if a new request removes or replaces an entry while another request is queued, depending on cleanup timing.
A 2-second client timeout can retry the payment independently of the coupon update and charge twice even if local coupon access is serialized.
A same-process concurrency test can pass while production cross-pod races remain untested.
result.better_alternative: Perform an atomic Postgres claim such as UPDATE coupons SET redemption_state='CLAIMED', order_id=$order, claim_token=$token, claimed_at=now() WHERE code=$code AND redemption_state='AVAILABLE', accepting only a request that updates one row. Enforce a unique coupon redemption invariant in the database, invoke chargeOrder with an order/payment idempotency key, and finalize the claim only after confirmed success; reconcile timed-out or ambiguous claims against payment state rather than automatically releasing them. This avoids locks across payment latency and does not depend on pod affinity.

falsification_probe.description: Run the redemption request concurrently against two separate service instances, preferably with distinct Node.js processes sharing the same Postgres database, using the same fresh coupon.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If both return success or both reach the charge operation, the process-local mutex is disproven. A correct database-enforced solution should return success exactly once and AlreadyUsed or the same idempotent result to the other request.

result.recommendation: Replace the process-local mutex with an atomic, database-backed claim, for example `updateMany` conditioned on `code` and `redeemedAt IS NULL`, storing a unique redemption/order token before charging. Use that token or an order/coupon idempotency key with the payment provider and finalize the coupon transactionally, while defining recovery for crashes or payment failures; test concurrency through separate service instances sharing PostgreSQL.
critical_assumptions: Coupons are shared across all Deployment replicas through the same PostgreSQL database.
A successful charge must be durifiably associated with the same coupon claim.
The payment provider supports idempotency or another reliable reconciliation mechanism.
Redeem requests can be retried with a stable order or redemption idempotency key.
material_risks: Each replica has a different mutex map, so simultaneous requests handled by different pods can both observe an unused coupon and both charge.
Pod termination, deployment rollout, or eviction releases no application state and defeats serialization guarantees.
A crash after charging but before setting `redeemedAt` leaves the coupon redeemable and can cause another charge on retry.
A concurrent unit test in one Node.js process cannot reproduce the production cross-pod race.
Locking only around the existing operations does not make the external charge and database update atomic.
result.better_alternative: Perform a conditional database update that atomically claims the coupon, requiring exactly one affected row; only the winner may charge. Persist a unique redemption token/order ID and use it as the payment idempotency key, then finalize `redeemedAt` transactionally, with compensating release or reconciliation for pre-charge failures and incomplete claims.

falsification_probe.description: Run the two-request race against two independently started coupon-service processes or two Kubernetes pods sharing the database, routing one request to each and recording calls to `chargeOrder`.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If both processes call `chargeOrder` for the same code, the process-local mutex is proven ineffective; a correct database-backed claim should allow exactly one process to claim it and reach the charge.

result.recommendation: Replace the in-process async mutex with an indexed atomic Postgres claim, such as an UPDATE guarded by redeemedAt IS NULL or an insert into a redemptions table with a unique coupon identifier, and require exactly one successful claimant before charging. Persist CLAIMED/SUCCESS/FAILED state and use a stable payment idempotency key derived from the coupon and order; a same-process concurrency test does not validate correctness across replicas or retries.
critical_assumptions: All redemption requests are handled by one process, with no multiple Kubernetes replicas, rolling deployments, or horizontal autoscaling.
The mutex is held across the complete check/update/payment sequence and cannot be interrupted by process termination.
Payment timeouts and retries can be safely handled without releasing the coupon before the provider's outcome is known.
The application can durably record and reconcile claim state.
The coupon code uniquely identifies the coupon and can be protected by a database uniqueness constraint.
material_risks: Two requests routed to different replicas can both observe the coupon as unused and redeem or charge it twice.
A process crash or pod eviction drops the mutex, allowing another request to proceed while the first payment may still complete.

Semi-synchronous cross-region replication is a possible separate enhancement if the measured latency cost is acceptable.

falsification_probe.description: Run one isolated game day that blocks all East-to-West database traffic, kills the East primary, and measure from failure injection to successful Rails reads and writes while recording failed or unacknowledged transactions, recovery duration, primary-host writability, and West-primary latency.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if the old primary remains independently writable, acknowledged writes are lost beyond the accepted bound, recovery exceeds 60 seconds, or normal Rails writes fail or materially breach latency/timeout limits through the promoted West replica.

result.recommendation: Keep automated Orchestrator recovery, but initially restrict it to the main East-primary cluster and prefer an East-local replica for host failures; reserve West promotion for confirmed East-region failure. Add reliable fencing so an isolated old primary cannot accept writes, and define the acceptable asynchronous RPO before enabling promotion regardless of region. Validate the complete detection-to-reconnect-and-write path, including ambiguous commits, under one minute; pseudo-GTID simplifies topology but does not establish freshness or prevent data loss.
critical_assumptions: Orchestrator can complete detection, candidate selection, promotion, and topology publication within the remaining 25 seconds after its 30-second trigger.
A Raft quorum will remain available throughout East database failures.
Orchestrator can reliably distinguish the freshest candidate, or the business explicitly accepts asynchronous replication loss.
The old primary can be fenced automatically at the host, network, or MySQL-access layer.
East application instances can reconnect to a West primary and tolerate roughly 60 ms database RTT.
material_risks: A network partition can produce dual writable primaries because Orchestrator consensus does not itself fence the old database.
Asynchronous promotion can lose acknowledged transactions; Raft and pseudo-GTID do not prevent this.
Selecting a West replica for an East host failure shifts every write across regions and may exceed latency or throughput limits.
Enabling recovery for all clusters simultaneously creates a correlated automation blast radius.
Consul updates or Rails connection recovery may finish after promotion, or retries may duplicate non-idempotent writes.

falsification_probe.description: In staging, partition the primary from Orchestrator while keeping a database client connected; after 35 seconds, attempt writes through both the old primary and the advertised replacement, while timing when a new write succeeds.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if the old primary accepts a conflicting write after replacement promotion, or if end-to-end writable recovery takes longer than 60 seconds. Success requires automatic fencing or refusal of old-primary writes, exactly one authoritative writer, and timely service rediscovery.

result.recommendation: Keep Orchestrator and Raft as the failover mechanism, but do not enable unqualified promotion of any replica across regions. Configure explicit candidate eligibility, split-brain/fencing protections, and Consul/application health-routing integration; define and test the accepted asynchronous-replication RPO, including writes during detection and promotion. Validate that East application hosts can reliably use a West primary and that recovery completes within the one-minute objective.
critical_assumptions: East application hosts have production-grade network connectivity and acceptable latency to a West MySQL primary.
Orchestrator is correctly integrated with the application's Consul-based primary discovery and can atomically publish the new endpoint.
The deployment has fencing or equivalent protection against an isolated old primary continuing to accept writes.
Promoting a cross-region asynchronous replica will lose no writes that the product requires to retain.
All clusters use compatible MySQL 5.7 binary logging, Pseudo-GTID, credentials, and replication settings for Orchestrator recovery.
material_risks: A 30-second reachability threshold can trigger failover during a transient partition while the East primary continues accepting writes, creating divergent primaries and irreversible data loss.
Asynchronous cross-region replication permits committed East writes to be absent from the West replica at promotion time; selecting the most advanced replica does not eliminate this RPO.
Promoting a West replica without verified East-to-West database routing or adequate client/network behavior can cause an extended application outage rather than sub-minute recovery.
Orchestrator's topology update alone does not guarantee that every Rails connection pool, Consul consumer, and connection-establishment path will follow the new primary.
Enabling automated recovery for all clusters without per-cluster safeguards can cause simultaneous or unsafe failovers during a regional event.

falsification_probe.description: Run a controlled game day with continuous, uniquely identifiable writes, kill the East primary, and measure from failure detection through successful application writes while checking the old primary, selected replica, Consul endpoint, and write continuity.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if writes accepted by the old primary are missing after promotion, the old primary remains writable, East clients cannot write to the promoted replica within the required interval, or Consul/application traffic does not converge to the new primary.

result.recommendation: Add explicit primary fencing before promotion and a Consul state machine that publishes the endpoint only after the promoted MySQL instance is writable and replication topology is stable. Restrict routine failover to deterministically prioritized East replicas, keep West as disaster recovery, and measure detection, promotion, and client reconnection convergence separately. Test acknowledged-write loss, transient stalls, stale replicas, manual topology changes, and connection-pool behavior rather than testing only host kills.
critical_assumptions: A supported fencing mechanism can revoke the failed primary's write capability before promotion.
Orchestrator's Raft quorum does not fence MySQL or prevent a surviving isolated primary from accepting writes.
Replica lag is low enough that selecting the most up-to-date replica does not lose acknowledged transactions.
Consul can atomically or sequentially gate endpoint publication on verified MySQL writability.
Applications and connection pools converge on a changed Consul endpoint without repeatedly retaining stale connections.
material_risks: An isolated primary may continue accepting writes after replica promotion, causing split brain and divergent data.
Asynchronous failover may silently lose acknowledged writes present only on the failed primary.
Service discovery may route clients before the promoted server is writable or fully reconfigured.
Selecting a West replica for an East failure introduces cross-region latency and exposes the normal path to remote replication lag.
Enabling automation for all clusters without region-specific candidate priorities and conflict controls could promote unsafe or geographically distant replicas.
result.better_alternative: Use fenced, Orchestrator-driven East-local failover with deterministic candidate priorities, reserve West for regional disaster recovery, and publish the Consul endpoint through an explicit post-promotion writability state machine.

falsification_probe.description: In staging, isolate one primary from Orchestrator and all replicas while continuing to execute successful local writes, then permit automated promotion and query both database identities for new writes.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is unsafe if the replica can be promoted while the isolated primary still accepts writes; safety requires the old primary to be reliably fenced before promotion.

result.recommendation: Do not enable unrestricted promotion of the West replica under asynchronous replication. Restrict automatic recovery to a fenced, recently verified East replica, enable semi-synchronous replication where supported, and explicitly integrate Orchestrator recovery with Consul plus stale-primary fencing. Permit West promotion only as an operator-approved, acknowledged-data-loss procedure; Raft consensus protects Orchestrator decisions but does not make asynchronous MySQL replication current or prevent a database split brain.
critical_assumptions: An East replica normally remains available when the East primary host fails, which is not stated.
Orchestrator is configured with a safe promotion candidate, fencing, recovery timeouts, and Consul hooks for every relevant cluster.
The application can route writes to a West-promoted primary over the existing network and tolerate approximately 60 ms plus additional connection latency.
Promoting an asynchronously replicated West node without losing acknowledged writes is acceptable, despite replication lag.
Consul updates and application client behavior will reliably converge within the one-minute objective.
material_risks: West promotion can lose committed writes because asynchronous replication may not have received them; choosing the apparently most advanced replica does not eliminate this.
A network partition or stalled primary can leave the old primary accepting writes after promotion unless storage/network fencing is enforced; Orchestrator Raft quorum does not fence MySQL.
Promoting a West node while application servers remain in East may create connectivity, latency, DNS/Consul propagation, and write-availability failures.
Applying automated recovery to all clusters without per-cluster safeguards can trigger simultaneous or incorrect promotions.
A 30-second detection threshold does not guarantee recovery under one minute after detection, topology repair, Consul propagation, and application reconnection.
result.better_alternative: Use Orchestrator automation only for a pre-approved East-local replica, configure semi-synchronous replication for East replicas, fence the failed primary before promotion, and have Consul publish a versioned primary endpoint. Keep West as an explicitly operator-invoked disaster-recovery path with documented possible data loss.

falsification_probe.description: During sustained writes to the East primary, record `SHOW SLAVE STATUS` on the West replica and execute a controlled primary failure followed by West promotion; compare acknowledged write IDs with rows present on the promoted replica.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If any acknowledged write is absent on the promoted West replica, or if East applications cannot route and commit writes to it within one minute, the proposed cross-region automated promotion fails the stated safety/availability objective.

result.recommendation: Retain automated Orchestrator recovery, but require explicit old-primary fencing, an approved promotion policy, pre-promotion topology/lag checks, and cluster-by-cluster canarying. Do not automatically select the most up-to-date replica regardless of region; use a designated preference and account for East application latency, replication lag, and a declared RPO.
critical_assumptions: A West promotion remains reachable from East application servers with acceptable latency and connection stability.
The old East primary can be conclusively fenced before the promoted replica accepts writes.
Orchestrator detection plus Raft election, promotion, replica reconfiguration, and discovery convergence consistently complete within 60 seconds.
The chosen replica's replication lag and connection state provide a tolerable committed-write RPO.
Orchestrator 3.x, MySQL 5.7, and pseudo-GTID behave correctly through these failure and recovery transitions.
material_risks: A network partition can trigger promotion without fencing the old primary, causing split brain and divergent writes.
Promoting a lagging West replica can lose committed transactions despite pseudo-GTID.
Automated reconfiguration can stall or partially complete, extending write unavailability or leaving inconsistent topology.
An unreachable West primary can make East applications fail or suffer unacceptable latency because service discovery alone does not ensure connectivity.
Applying automation to all clusters at once can create simultaneous elections, discovery churn, and an operator overload during the failure.

falsification_probe.description: In a production-like staging environment, run one isolated end-to-end game day: continuously commit marked writes, hard-kill the East primary, record write errors and failure timing, and verify fencing, selected replica, data present, topology repair, and application recovery.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is supported only if there is a single authoritative primary, no unexplained lost acknowledged writes, all application writes recover within 60 seconds, replicas converge, and service discovery settles consistently; a split brain, unacceptable loss, or recovery beyond 60 seconds falsifies it.

result.recommendation: Keep explicit date-named versions and account-level defaults, but do not make the latest response plus reverse delta modules the sole compatibility mechanism. Implement independently maintained, contract-tested serializers or canonical versioned response builders for each supported version, and restrict request transformations to provably invertible changes. Preserve the current contract as the default, allow explicit opt-in upgrades, and define a long-lived deprecation and telemetry policy.
critical_assumptions: Every integration can be reliably associated with a stable account identity; shared accounts, anonymous clients, and multiple client generations may not share one version.
All historical request and response semantics can be reconstructed accurately, including validation, defaults, error behavior, ordering, nullability, and authorization-visible fields.
Each breaking change is safely composable and reversible when transforming the latest request and response into every older version.
Additive changes are genuinely backward-compatible for the observed client population, including clients that reject unknown fields or use strict schemas.
The account's first request is an appropriate compatibility pin and does not prevent integrations from receiving later security fixes or required non-breaking updates.
material_risks: A request transformation may be impossible to invert when newer versions add required semantics, remove accepted inputs, alter validation, or change authorization; the latest model can therefore not safely represent old contracts.
A single account may contain several integrations with different clients or release histories, causing an incorrect default version and widespread breakage.
Delta chains can drift or become order-dependent, producing incorrect combinations even when individual modules pass unit tests.
Pinning new integrations to the version at first request may indefinitely preserve obsolete behavior, while header overrides can let clients accidentally select incompatible behavior.
Changing the default or applying additive fields can break strict consumers, while retaining every version increases serialization, monitoring, and security-maintenance costs.
result.better_alternative: Use explicit versioned contracts with independent serializers and request decoders, generated from or validated against shared contract fixtures. Keep the current version as the compatibility default, introduce a new dated version only for a documented breaking contract, and migrate callers using usage telemetry, sandbox testing, and a multi-year support window rather than account-first-request pinning alone.

falsification_probe.description: Select one representative current account and replay a corpus of its historical requests and expected responses through the proposed latest-model-plus-reverse-module pipeline across at least three proposed versions; compare exact bodies, headers, status codes, validation errors, and ordering.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If any non-invertible semantic difference, incorrect field combination, ordering/header mismatch, or untestable account identity appears, the chain-based compatibility guarantee is disproven and independent version handlers are required.

result.recommendation: Keep date-based account pinning, but do not make arbitrary chained transformations the sole compatibility mechanism. Define an explicit compatibility contract for every supported version, use versioned boundary serializers or adapters where transformations are lossy, and specify the exact semantics and authorization of per-request version overrides. Maintain conformance tests that replay real historical request/response fixtures.
critical_assumptions: Every breaking change can be represented by a deterministic, tested transformation between the latest canonical model and each supported historical version.
Transformations preserve payment semantics, validation behavior, error codes, and security-relevant fields, not merely field names and JSON structure.
The service can retain and execute an unbounded chain of version modules without unacceptable latency and memory costs.
Account-level pinning is durable, authenticated, and independent of client headers or migration/import behavior.
Clients that send a version header understand that it may change the response contract and cannot accidentally bypass the account's supported compatibility policy.
material_risks: A removed, merged, or semantically changed field may be impossible to reconstruct from the latest response, causing silent corruption or incorrect payment behavior.
Request transformations may not reproduce the validation and authorization behavior expected by historical clients, creating security or financial risk.
The transformation chain will grow with every breaking change, increasing request latency, deployment complexity, and the chance that old versions drift or are accidentally broken.
A header override can route production traffic to an incompatible version unless version selection is explicitly constrained and observable.
Generated changelogs and unit tests do not guarantee compatibility with the roughly 50k integrations' actual historical payload and error-handling behavior.
result.better_alternative: Use the same date-version negotiation and account pinning, but maintain explicit versioned API contracts and serializers/adapters at the service boundary, with a canonical internal model between them. This avoids requiring a lossy global reverse transformation chain while preserving exact historical behavior.

falsification_probe.description: Create a fixture for one irreversible breaking change, such as splitting a legacy amount-and-currency object into separate fields, then run both the historical request through the latest adapter and the latest response through the historical adapter.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The test should produce byte-equivalent historical response behavior and semantically equivalent request validation, including errors; any missing field, changed meaning, or validation discrepancy falsifies the transformation-chain design.

result.recommendation: Keep explicit date-based versions, but make each version an immutable contract rather than deriving it from a mutable latest response through a chain of reverse transformations. Define routing, supported-version policy, request/response golden tests, and telemetry-based deprecation; require a new major version for semantic changes, including payment behavior. Do not let an unvalidated per-request header silently change an account's contract.
critical_assumptions: Every client and integration can reliably propagate and honor an explicit version selector, including through gateways, SDKs, proxies, and webhooks.
An account is a valid compatibility boundary, so all clients for an account can use the same pinned representation.
Reverse transformation modules can reproduce every historical request and response contract exactly, including validation and error behavior.
The organization can retain and test all historical transformation modules indefinitely.
Payment and security semantics can be transformed compatibly without changing authorization, idempotency, or settlement meaning.
material_risks: A mutable latest representation plus reverse modules allows an internal change to inadvertently alter a supposedly immutable historical contract.
Clients sharing an account may receive an unexpected representation, especially when the per-request override bypasses account pinning.
Composition and ordering bugs across multiple breaking-change modules can produce incorrect fields, requests, or errors.
Without field- and client-level telemetry and a published support window, old versions may be removed while active integrations still depend on them.
Same-shaped semantic changes to payments or authorization could bypass version checks and cause financial or security incidents.
result.better_alternative: Use explicit immutable major versions with dedicated serializers/contracts and contract tests; allow additive evolution within a major version, and use telemetry, a published deprecation window, and a controlled migration path.

falsification_probe.description: Create golden fixtures for at least one existing v1 client covering two historical breaking changes, then apply the proposed newest-to-oldest transformation chain and compare the complete request, response, validation errors, and payment semantics against the v1 contract.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any mismatch, missing error behavior, or semantic payment discrepancy falsifies the claim that the transformation chain preserves the immutable contract; an exact match would support the architecture but would not resolve routing, telemetry, or deprecation gaps.

result.recommendation: Retain date-based versioning, but make the negotiated version an explicit, durable API contract rather than silently binding it to each account's first request. Define header/default negotiation, precedence and authorization; maintain immutable golden contract fixtures for every supported version; and require compatibility tests proving that the complete downgrade chain reproduces each prior wire format, including error responses and additive changes.
critical_assumptions: Account identity and its negotiated version can be stored reliably across service migrations and backend rewrites.
Every breaking request and response change can be expressed as a deterministic, reversible adapter step.
The latest internal representation remains serializable while all older adapter chains execute.
Headers are already available to all clients and can safely override the account-level version.
The cost and latency of increasingly long transformation chains remain operationally acceptable.
material_risks: Silent account pinning can route traffic to a legacy contract unexpectedly, especially after account migration, credential changes, or first-request races.
Individually correct transformations can fail composably when multiple changes touch the same field, enum, nullability rule, or error path.
A new internal model or serialization failure can break old clients before downgrade modules have an opportunity to translate it.
Clients may send arbitrary or stale version headers, creating cache, routing, security, and support inconsistencies.
Calling all additive changes backward-compatible may still violate strict consumers if fields, status codes, or default values change.

falsification_probe.description: Create immutable golden request/response fixtures for every currently supported API version, pass representative valid and invalid requests through the actual negotiation and full transformation chain, and compare the emitted wire output to those fixtures.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The design is viable only if all fixtures match without account-specific special cases and the suite covers the longest supported chain; any unexplained mismatch, panic, or unbounded latency falsifies the claimed compatibility guarantee.

result.recommendation: Retain date-based versions and account pinning, but replace the unbounded transformation chain with explicit version-specific serializers, validators, and request adapters sharing stable domain logic. Define a durable, region-consistent version-selection policy, restrict and log overrides, and require contract tests against representative traffic for every supported version before release. Treat nullability, numeric precision, error envelopes, idempotency, and request semantics as first-class compatibility concerns.
critical_assumptions: A stable account identifier is available on the first request and remains consistently available during authentication, migration, and failover.
All externally visible behavior can be isolated at the serialization boundary without version-specific business workflows or side effects.
The team can maintain version-specific contract tests and compatibility modules for every supported contract indefinitely.
Historical transformations are sufficiently composable that applying them newest-to-oldest preserves semantics and intermediate states do not cause failures.
Clients can safely use a version header without weakening authentication, authorization, idempotency, or replay protections.
material_risks: A transform may be mathematically reversible for simple field mappings while irreversibly changing validation, authorization, side effects, or error behavior for requests.
Module ordering or version-selection bugs could expose the wrong payment schema or execute version-incompatible operations.
Account pins may diverge across regions or be reset during account migration, creating inconsistent behavior for the same integration.
Unbounded chains will increase latency and debugging complexity until a change in one module breaks responses for many older versions.
Uncontrolled header overrides may let clients bypass their pinned compatibility contract or select an unsupported version.
result.better_alternative: Use explicit major-version entry points, serializers, and validators that map a shared canonical domain result into each contract. Share stable business logic, but make every externally observable difference visible and independently testable rather than accumulating compositional backward transforms.

falsification_probe.description: Implement one representative legacy contract and two subsequent breaking changes in a small proof of concept, then run contract tests and replay sanitized production examples through both the proposed reverse-transform chain and a version-specific serializer.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposed chain is falsified if any response or request cannot match the recorded legacy contract exactly, requires version-specific business context or side effects, or fails because of intermediate-version behavior; a version-specific serializer that matches all fixtures would confirm the alternative.

result.recommendation: Retain versioned serialization modules, but do not silently pin an account to the version of its first request: provide a stable legacy baseline and an explicit, observable account-level migration mechanism. Define “additive” narrowly, require both request and response golden-contract tests across every supported version, and commit to maintaining historical modules for the required support window.
critical_assumptions: One account corresponds closely enough to one integration contract; otherwise first-request pinning gives unrelated clients incompatible schemas.
Every breaking change can be inverted or modeled so latest-to-legacy responses and legacy-to-latest requests are semantically complete.
The module chain has deterministic ordering and can be executed efficiently on the request hot path.
Clients can distinguish the version header from ordinary per-request experimentation and will not assume header overrides migrate the account.
The team will maintain old modules, dependencies, and contract tests indefinitely or through a formally enforced support policy.
material_risks: Different integrations sharing an account receive the same pinned schema, causing immediate cross-client breakage.
A new version changes the representation of all accounts pinned to that date, so a bug fix or serializer refactor can become an unintended breaking change.
Chains grow linearly with version count and may become request-latency or availability liabilities; transformations may also be lossy or semantically non-invertible.
Calling a change additive may still break strict clients, alter field meaning, or change nullability, enum handling, ordering, and error behavior.
Clients can test headers forever without an account migration path, leaving operational complexity permanently unresolved.
result.better_alternative: Use explicit, independently defined DTO/serializer contracts for each breaking version rather than making the latest internal shape the canonical representation and reconstructing old contracts through chained transforms. A shared normalized application result can feed these serializers, avoiding lossy downgrade logic while preserving account-level version selection.

falsification_probe.description: Build a representative request/response fixture per supported version, map each fixture into the latest internal shape, run it through the complete downgrade chain, and compare the result with the original version's golden contract byte-for-byte or by strict JSON semantic comparison.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any missing, renamed, retyped, reordered, nullability, enum, or error-response difference—or any legacy request pair that cannot be mapped into the latest shape without information loss—would falsify the claim that the module chain is a safe general versioning strategy.

result.recommendation: The versioning direction is sound, but define versioning at the integration or API-credential level rather than the account level, and specify the exact negotiation, pinning, and override semantics. Require every breaking change to provide deterministic, independently tested forward and inverse adapters, preserve a versioned golden-contract test suite, and establish deprecation and sunset policies; do not classify all additive changes as automatically safe without validating request and payment-semantics compatibility.
critical_assumptions: An account may contain multiple independent integrations whose clients require different API versions.
Every breaking response and request change can be represented as a deterministic, reversible or explicitly lossy adapter.
The service can retain and execute a growing chain of adapters for all supported versions.
Clients cannot accidentally or maliciously select an incompatible version through the override header.
The organization can operate version-specific schemas, documentation, tests, telemetry, and support for several years.
material_risks: Account-level pinning can force unrelated integrations onto the same version or make the first request from a new client unexpectedly select a much newer contract.
A header override can return a response shape that does not match the request's effective version, causing client parsing or payment-processing failures.
Transforming the latest internal representation backward can silently lose information or alter payment semantics when a newer change removes or redefines fields.
The adapter chain can grow indefinitely and make weekly releases slower or riskier unless ordering, ownership, performance budgets, and version retirement are controlled.
Assuming additive changes are safe can break clients when added response fields trigger strict deserializers or when optional request fields change validation, defaults, or business behavior.

falsification_probe.description: Create a golden compatibility test containing a representative v1 payment request and response, introduce a representative v2 breaking change, and run both through the proposed adapter chain and contract tests.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if the v1 request or response cannot be reproduced byte-for-byte or semantically after the v2 change, or if adapter ordering/overrides produce a response that does not match the effective request version.

result.recommendation: Retain account pinning only as a rollout mechanism, but define immutable, explicitly versioned response and request contracts with independent serializers and contract tests. Do not rely solely on a chain of reverse transformations: preserve the legacy default contract, restrict per-request overrides to controlled testing or explicitly negotiated access, and document ownership, compatibility guarantees, telemetry, and retirement criteria.
critical_assumptions: Every integration can be reliably associated with an account before its first request, including dormant, private, or multi-account clients.
All breaking changes can be represented as composable, reversible transformations from the latest shape.
Existing clients tolerate additive fields or the transformation chain explicitly removes fields they reject.
Clients cannot use the upgrade header to obtain an incompatible shape in production.
The latest internal model contains enough information to reconstruct every supported historical request and response.
material_risks: An unknown or incorrectly identified account receives the latest shape, breaking existing clients despite the claimed compatibility.
A request/response transformation omits a breaking change or loses information, producing invalid legacy payloads or altering writes.
Additive fields cause strict client schema validation failures because no new major version is introduced.
Per-request header overrides make the contract account-dependent and can accidentally expose an incompatible representation to production clients.
Accumulated transformation modules create ordering, maintenance, and testing costs without clear version ownership or retirement rules.
result.better_alternative: Use explicit major-version contracts at the serialization boundary, with separate legacy serializers/adapters and automated contract tests; optionally pin accounts to a version for migration, but do not make account state the sole definition of API compatibility.

falsification_probe.description: Replay one representative captured legacy client request against a fresh or unmapped account using a strict legacy response schema, with and without the upgrade header.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the server cannot return the documented legacy shape deterministically, or if an unapproved header changes the production contract, the proposal is unsafe for existing integrations.

result.recommendation: Retain explicit, durable API versions, but do not pin an account on its first request or rely indefinitely on a chain of reverse transformations. Define versioning at the integration/credential level, support deliberate migration and rollback, and maintain independent versioned contracts (or serializers) with conformance, performance, and security tests. Specify precedence for account, credential, and per-request version headers, and make unsupported or unsafe overrides fail explicitly.
critical_assumptions: An account is an appropriate proxy for a stable integration identity; shared accounts, credential rotation, and account migrations may invalidate this.
Every breaking change is losslessly reversible from the latest response and request shapes, including validation, authorization, and payment semantics.
The cumulative transformation chain remains fast, correct, and maintainable as weekly changes accumulate over years.
Clients will tolerate additive fields and other non-breaking changes without version negotiation.
Historical behavior can be preserved without retaining sensitive data or preserving implementation details that later become unsafe.
material_risks: A first-request pin can freeze unrelated integrations together or silently apply the wrong contract after account ownership, credentials, or tenancy changes.
Reverse transformations may be impossible or lossy when internal refactors remove information, merge fields, alter validation, or change authorization behavior.
Applying many modules on every request can create latency and outage risk; one incorrect module can corrupt payments or weaken security for all old clients.
Header overrides can let clients select incompatible request/response behavior without an authenticated, auditable compatibility policy.
Old versions and transformation code may accumulate indefinitely, making supply-chain, dependency, privacy, and incident-response burdens unacceptable.
result.better_alternative: Use independently implemented, contract-tested versioned API representations selected by an explicit integration/credential version, with a bounded compatibility layer and a published deprecation/migration process. Prefer adapters between stable internal commands and each API version over transforming the latest wire shape backward.

falsification_probe.description: Build one representative legacy request/response contract and run the full production transformation chain in property-based and replay tests, including a breaking change that removes or renames fields, adds validation, and changes authorization behavior.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is confirmed only if every supported version produces byte-for-byte or semantically equivalent legacy behavior with bounded latency, complete validation/authorization parity, and no unresolved data loss; any mismatch falsifies the reverse-chain approach.

result.recommendation: Replace account-level first-request pinning and cumulative reverse adapters with explicitly versioned request schemas and response serializers per supported contract. Select the version from a stable integration or credential identity, default unversioned clients to a frozen legacy contract, and govern every change—including errors, pagination, nullability, and status codes—with contract tests and telemetry.
critical_assumptions: An account is equivalent to one integration and therefore has one meaningful compatibility version.
Every historical behavior can be reconstructed losslessly by ordered field-level transformations from the latest response.
The complete external API surface is intercepted by the serialization layer, not merely object fields.
Clients testing an override can bypass the account pin without creating inconsistent session, cache, or idempotency behavior.
Keeping and evaluating an ever-growing adapter chain for years will remain cheaper and safer than maintaining version-specific serializers.
material_risks: Shared accounts, administrative first requests, or credential rotation can pin the wrong clients and immediately break unrelated integrations.
Weekly adapters accumulate ordering, interaction, and performance costs, making historical behavior difficult to reproduce correctly.
Changes to errors, pagination, status codes, nullability, or semantics may bypass modules and silently break clients.
Calling all additive changes safe can break strict deserializers, generated clients, signatures, or downstream field validators.
Incorrect or inconsistent override handling can produce different payloads for the same operation and undermine supportability.
result.better_alternative: Use immutable date-named contract versions with separate request parsing and response serialization or generated DTOs. Preserve the current unversioned contract indefinitely, introduce a new explicitly versioned contract, and generate compatibility fixtures and documentation from the same definitions.

falsification_probe.description: Run a read-only account/client analysis joining API credentials or integration identifiers to account IDs, then count distinct clients per account and classify which client made each account's first API request.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any material population of accounts serving multiple clients, or first requests coming from shared administrative/test credentials, falsifies account-level first-request pinning. One client per account with stable first-request attribution would validate that part of the proposal, though not the long-term adapter chain.

result.recommendation: Keep versioned representations, but pin versions to an explicit credential or client identity rather than the account, and define deterministic behavior for unauthenticated or shared credentials. Define transformations as a compatibility specification, prohibit reordering, and require golden contract tests covering full requests, responses, errors, nulls, enums, timestamps, and idempotency; additive changes must still follow strict-compatibility policy.
critical_assumptions: Each account corresponds to one integration with a stable, correctly identified API client.
The initial-version assignment is atomic, durable, and already possible to define for every existing integration.
Each breaking change can be inverted without losing information or altering payment behavior.
Version modules remain ordered, composable, and backward-compatible with every previously pinned version.
Additive changes are safe for all clients, including strict decoders, enum consumers, webhook verifiers, and signature implementations.
material_risks: One account may have multiple clients, credentials, or regional integrations, causing an unexpected version to be pinned or applied.
Lossy or non-commutative transformations can corrupt payment fields even when apparent shape tests pass.
A first request after rollout may pin legacy expectations to the new date version, while account creation or transfer may silently change the selected contract.
Changing errors, null handling, enums, timestamps, idempotency, or signature inputs is likely to be overlooked if modules are organized only by response shape.
Every pinned version makes the service execute an increasingly long transformation chain, increasing latency and coupling future releases to years-old modules.

falsification_probe.description: Run a representative captured production corpus of sanitized payment requests and responses through the proposed transformation pipeline for every currently observed account version, and diff byte-equivalent parsed JSON plus status, headers, and relevant idempotency behavior against the existing contract.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any fixture mismatch that cannot be explained by an explicitly approved breaking change would prove the chain is not behavior-preserving; a complete match supports the mechanism but not yet its future maintainability.

result.recommendation: Keep date-based versions and per-account pinning, but do not make the latest representation the sole source for all older versions. Define a versioned canonical representation or generate serializers/adapters from the internal model for each supported version, with explicit compatibility fixtures and an enumerated request/response contract. Treat lossy or semantically irreversible changes as requiring a new representation rather than assuming a reverse transformation can recover old behavior.
critical_assumptions: Every response shape required by an older version can be derived from the latest internal response, including fields removed or semantically changed by later releases.
Old client requests can be transformed into the latest request semantics without ambiguity or loss, including validation, defaults, and idempotency behavior.
Account identity is available before the first request so the initial version pin is deterministic and cannot be bypassed or reset.
Clients that omit a version header remain pinned indefinitely, and an explicit header can be handled without changing the account's persistent pin.
Additive changes are demonstrably non-breaking for the supported client population, including strict deserializers and enum/schema validators.
material_risks: A change that removes or overwrites data can make backward response transformation impossible, causing silent incorrect payments responses for pinned integrations.
Request adapters may map multiple old inputs to one latest input or reject inputs that previously succeeded, breaking payment creation and retries.
A transformation chain can produce a superficially correct shape with incorrect business semantics, which is particularly damaging for financial APIs.
The number and interaction of version-change modules will grow indefinitely; ordering, ownership, and cross-version regressions could make weekly releases unsafe.
Relying on additive compatibility without an explicit contract can break integrations using strict schemas, generated clients, or validation libraries.

falsification_probe.description: Create a fixture for a supported old version in which a later release removes a response field or changes its meaning, then run the proposed newest-to-old transformation chain against the latest fixture and compare the result byte-for-byte and semantically with the old contract.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the old field cannot be reconstructed or the reconstructed value differs under the old contract, the latest-shape-plus-reverse-transform design is unsound for that valid version history.

result.recommendation: Keep date-based versions, but do not pin clients implicitly by account or derive the target representation by transforming the latest response. Route requests to explicit, independently maintained version-specific DTOs and serializer adapters, with additive-only changes inside a version and a new version for incompatible shape or semantic changes. Add endpoint/client/field telemetry, contract tests, deprecation dates, and a multi-year migration window before retirement; treat header overrides as migration tooling rather than the default compatibility mechanism.
critical_assumptions: The transform chain can faithfully reverse every breaking change, including changes to defaults, nullability, enums, timestamps, status codes, and error shapes.
Producing the latest internal shape before transforming it does not alter business semantics or authorization behavior for older representations.
Every integration can be reliably associated with an account and supplied with a valid version header when behavior differs.
Serialization modules can be composed in either direction without creating divergent business logic or unbounded maintenance costs.
The organization can observe endpoint, version, client, field, and undocumented behavior well enough to establish safe retirement dates.
material_risks: A latest-shape change involving semantics, defaults, or error behavior may be impossible to reverse reliably, causing silent client breakage despite passing shape-focused module tests.
First-request account pinning can assign the wrong version when accounts are shared, migrated, recreated, or contain integrations with different release schedules.
Header-based overrides can allow clients to request unsupported representations or bypass the intended compatibility contract.
Unobserved undocumented dependencies may break during transformation because the proposal does not require consumer telemetry or strict contract tests.
A chain of reverse transformations can become order-dependent, expensive, or difficult to retire, while old clients remain blocked on long-term dual maintenance.
result.better_alternative: Use explicit API versions with version-specific DTOs and serializer adapters, preserving the current version as the default for existing clients and allowing explicit negotiation or migration headers. Maintain a compatibility matrix and golden contract tests for every supported version, and retire versions only after client- and field-level telemetry, published deprecation dates, and a multi-year migration window.

falsification_probe.description: Create a golden contract test for one existing pinned client, then introduce an incompatible latest-version change to a response default, error status, nullable field, and enum value and run the old-version contract suite.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if the reverse transformation cannot reproduce the exact legacy status, headers, JSON shape, nullability, enum, and semantic behavior, or if the request path changes business outcomes; this confirms that latest-shape-plus-reverse-transform is not a safe compatibility boundary.

result.recommendation: Retain explicit date-based versions, but do not use an account’s first request as the authoritative version and do not derive every legacy response from the latest representation. Freeze a legacy contract, negotiate an explicit version per request, normalize each version into a stable internal model, and generate or verify versioned representations through contract tests; treat additive changes as compatible only against a documented compatibility policy.
critical_assumptions: Every integration can be reliably associated with an account, and multiple independent integrations under one account can safely share a default version.
The latest internal model retains enough information to reconstruct every supported historical response exactly.
A permanent multi-year support window, including monitoring, security fixes, and compatibility testing, is operationally funded.
Clients accept date-version negotiation through a header without exposing unrelated account versions.
Historical response changes are sufficiently independent and composable to implement as an ordered chain.
material_risks: The first request may come from an internal caller, shared infrastructure, a new integration, or a client already sending a version header, causing an incorrect irreversible default.
Transforming the latest shape backward can silently corrupt payments data when fields are deleted, renamed, rounded, defaulted, or represented with different semantics.
Request and response transformations can be non-invertible, while weekly changes will increase chain latency and the probability of ordering or dependency defects.
Calling all additive changes safe may break strict generated clients, pagination consumers, enum handling, or consumers that reject unknown fields.
Supporting many versions indefinitely creates a large security and maintenance surface; account-level pinning can also prevent timely migration without a controlled opt-in process.
result.better_alternative: Use immutable, explicitly negotiated API representations with a frozen legacy baseline. Convert supported request versions into a canonical payment command model, render responses from version-specific schemas or isolated translators, and maintain golden contract tests plus a published deprecation and migration policy. An account-level default may exist, but it must be preconfigured for existing accounts and remain overridable explicitly.

falsification_probe.description: Select one representative response for every historical breaking change and replay it through the proposed newest-to-oldest module chain, comparing the result with the exact previously published contract.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The approach is falsified if any legacy field, value, nullability, ordering, pagination, or error semantic cannot be reproduced exactly from the latest shape; success across all historical contracts would confirm the core downgrade mechanism but not the account-pinning policy.

result.recommendation: Retain date-named versions and module documentation/testing, but replace account pinning and long reverse transform chains with explicit immutable version-specific serializers or contract mappers. Preserve a stable default for clients that send no version, allow explicit opt-in testing, and make unknown or conflicting versions observable rather than silently changing behavior.
critical_assumptions: The gateway and all supported SDKs propagate a version header consistently across retries, redirects, and subrequests.
Every supported external version can be reconstructed deterministically from the latest internal representation.
Compatibility can be decided from the actual external contract, including validation, errors, pagination, and money semantics, not schema shape alone.
Transform latency and operational complexity remain acceptable as the number of versions and modules grows.
Additive changes will be governed by a precise contract and compatibility test suite.
material_risks: An account can send different version requirements per endpoint or request, while one first-request pin produces silent, inconsistent contracts.
Sequential bidirectional modules can introduce ordering, coverage, latency, and correctness defects; omitted or unsupported changes are especially dangerous on payments.
Clients that propagate or duplicate custom headers may accidentally override the account default and test an unintended version.
A header override can expose preview behavior in production, altering payment validation or business behavior.
Schema-only classification may label semantic or validation changes as additive, breaking integrations without creating a new version.
result.better_alternative: Use a stable legacy representation as the default and expose date-named immutable contracts explicitly. Generate them through direct version-specific serializers where practical, or bounded compatibility mappers near the serialization boundary; validate each contract with captured or producer-consumer fixtures and record effective-version telemetry per request.

falsification_probe.description: Run a small cross-client replay against a staging endpoint using the 20 most common SDK, browser, proxy, and server patterns: test retries, redirects, nested requests, and duplicate headers, then assert the backend receives exactly the intended version everywhere.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The approach is falsified if any normal client loses, duplicates, or changes the version during propagation, or if the same account legitimately requires multiple external contracts for the same endpoint; this would make account-level pinning unsafe and require explicit per-request or per-operation selection.

result.recommendation: Keep the expedited Quicksilver path and global log-only phase, but require deterministic PCRE safety/latency tests, mandatory peer approval, per-rule automatic abort thresholds, and a rehearsed kill switch before activation. After logging, block on a small traffic slice for 5-10 minutes and check errors, p99 latency, CPU, and rule match volume before global blocking; emergency execution time should be capped and measured end to end.
critical_assumptions: The rule engine bounds regex execution, or CI can reliably detect catastrophic backtracking using adversarial inputs.
Quicksilver can activate log mode and later blocking globally within minutes, with consistent version state at every PoP.
Log evaluation adds acceptable CPU and latency even when a request produces many matches.
Match-volume telemetry is available within minutes and has useful PoP-, customer-, and traffic-normalized baselines.
A single rule can be disabled immediately without disrupting the rest of the WAF configuration.
material_risks: A vulnerable or pathological PCRE consumes enough CPU in log mode to degrade customer traffic before any match threshold is evaluated.
A broad signature produces many benign matches; the ten-minute observation either misses rare events or causes an extended global denial when switched to block.
A bad configuration is partially activated across PoPs, yielding inconsistent protection and difficult incident diagnosis.
Telemetry is delayed, aggregated too coarsely, or unavailable during the disclosure, leaving the team to block without production evidence.
The process is rushed, omitting security review or rollback verification precisely when operational pressure is highest.
result.better_alternative: Use the proposed path as the standard, but define it as a gated incident release: static and adversarial regex validation, peak-load replay, global log mode for 10 minutes, a 5-10 minute blocking canary, then global block. This is a modification rather than a separate architecture because it preserves the proposal's low operational complexity while adding protections for false positives and rollout failure.

falsification_probe.description: Replay the candidate regex plus worst-case encodings and match-heavy inputs through the actual PCRE engine in log mode under representative peak-load concurrency, while measuring proxy CPU, p99 latency, and per-rule match throughput.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if log-mode evaluation can breach the defined CPU or latency budget, cannot terminate within the rule-execution timeout, or produces enough matches/events that telemetry or rollback cannot process within minutes.

result.recommendation: Keep the expedited Quicksilver path, but do not allow an arbitrary CI-passing PCRE to enter the inline request path or automatically block globally after a fixed 10-minute observation period. Require a strict evaluation-time/CPU budget, reject unsafe regex constructs, preserve an independently controlled kill switch and atomic rollback, and validate benign traffic volume and latency during the log period before enabling blocking.
critical_assumptions: The WAF engine enforces a hard per-rule evaluation timeout and can safely terminate pathological PCRE execution.
Quicksilver updates are versioned and can be rolled back consistently across all PoPs within minutes.
CI's benign-request corpus is representative enough to detect likely false positives before global enforcement.
Log-mode evaluation has a bounded CPU and memory cost comparable to block-mode evaluation.
A global configuration update can be gated, audited, and reversed without waiting for the normal staged pipeline.
material_risks: A catastrophic-backtracking or otherwise pathological regex could consume proxy CPU, degrade or halt all customer traffic because WAF evaluation is inline and proxies are already CPU-bound.
Ten minutes of match-volume observation may miss low-frequency false positives, false negatives, regional traffic differences, or application-specific behavior.
Automatic global blocking could deny legitimate requests across every customer immediately, with no safe mechanism to disable the rule quickly.
Configuration propagation or version skew could produce inconsistent enforcement across PoPs and make rollback unreliable.
The safety check may itself overload the request path if log mode materially increases latency or creates large match/event volumes.

falsification_probe.description: Run each candidate PCRE against the production benign corpus and representative attack payloads using the production WAF engine, with a hard timeout, while measuring p99 evaluation latency and CPU time.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if any CI-passing rule exhibits superlinear execution, exceeds the proxy's defined per-request CPU/latency budget, or causes the corpus run to approach the timeout; otherwise this supports retaining the expedited path with the stated safeguards.

result.recommendation: Retain global log mode as an expedited detection lane, but require preflight regex-complexity and worst-case CPU benchmarks plus benign-regression testing before promotion. Promote to block through automated 1%, 10%, 50%, and 100% cohorts with latency, error, CPU, match-rate, and false-positive gates, and preserve an atomic, tested global rollback to the last known-good ruleset.
critical_assumptions: Candidate regexes cannot cause pathological CPU usage on production proxy hardware.
The CI payload and benign-request corpora represent production attacks and legitimate traffic.
Quicksilver can atomically roll back the ruleset on every machine within the required window.
A ten-minute global log interval provides enough traffic and representative PoP coverage for reliable promotion decisions.
The rule-management system supports automated cohort control and managed-rule rollback.
material_risks: A catastrophic regex can overload proxies even in log mode because evaluation remains in the inline request path.
A false-positive rule can block legitimate customers globally before cohort-level safeguards detect it.
Ten minutes may omit low-volume PoPs, customers, payload variants, and benign edge cases.
Promotion or rollback performed manually may miss the one-hour objective.
An unsafe rule could become fleet-wide before aggregate match and error signals reveal the problem.
result.better_alternative: Use a narrowly scoped emergency mitigation immediately, deploy the production rule globally in log mode, and then promote it through minute-scale cohorts with automated safety gates. Require a known-good signed configuration, regex complexity limits, representative benign testing, and a tested one-click global rollback.

falsification_probe.description: Benchmark each candidate regex on production proxy hardware using generated worst-case inputs plus the CI payload and benign corpora, while measuring request latency and CPU.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if any input causes material CPU saturation, latency inflation, or unacceptable error rates; otherwise the benchmark clears the most immediate catastrophic-regression risk, though production cohort gates are still required.

result.recommendation: Retain the expedited path, but require versioned, signed configuration with local schema/resource validation, an automated global kill switch, and staged enforcement that still completes within one hour. Do not treat CI corpus success or ten minutes of low log volume as sufficient evidence of safety, because benign traffic may be absent or insufficiently represented and catastrophic PCRE backtracking remains possible.
critical_assumptions: Quicksilver can atomically distribute versioned WAF configuration to every proxy within the required latency.
Every proxy can reject invalid, incompatible, or computationally unsafe rules before activation.
The CI benign-request corpus is representative enough to detect likely false positives.
Ten minutes of traffic across all PoPs provides statistically meaningful coverage.
A rule can be disabled and previous configuration restored automatically within minutes.
material_risks: A false-positive rule could block legitimate customer traffic at every edge simultaneously.
A PCRE pattern with pathological backtracking could saturate already CPU-bound proxies; log mode still executes the regex.
A malformed or incompatible configuration could cause proxy reload failures or inconsistent enforcement.
Low observed match volume could conceal false positives because attack types and benign traffic vary by customer and PoP.
A partial Quicksilver distribution or failed flip could leave the fleet exposed or produce an unreviewable mixed state.
result.better_alternative: Publish a signed, versioned rule bundle with a precomputed PCRE complexity/resource limit; validate and benchmark it on proxy builds, enable observation on a small representative canary for several minutes, then automatically progress through 1%, 10%, and 100% block enforcement within the one-hour objective. Continuously compare match rates, latency, CPU, errors, and representative benign traffic, with automatic rollback on any threshold breach.

falsification_probe.description: Replay a production-representative benign request trace plus the CI payload corpus through the exact proxy/WAF build, measuring incremental p99 latency and CPU while enabling the proposed rule in log mode.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if any single rule exceeds the defined per-request CPU/latency budget, causes PCRE resource growth with input length, or matches representative benign traffic at a rate that would create material customer impact.

result.recommendation: Retain Quicksilver-based acceleration, but classify rules by confidence and deploy high-confidence signatures directly to block while broad rules use log mode and selected-PoP canaries. Before rollout, enforce regex complexity limits and per-rule CPU/latency budgets; automatically revert on proxy health, customer error-rate, or match-distribution thresholds, with a pretested global kill switch.
critical_assumptions: Passing the fixed CI corpus is strong enough to bound catastrophic false positives across production traffic.
