All proxies have enough spare CPU to evaluate new log-mode rules during peak traffic without degrading TLS or HTTP processing.
Quicksilver provides sufficiently fast, atomic, version-consistent mode changes and global rollback.
Central match-volume telemetry is timely and complete enough to detect harmful rules within the ten-minute window.
A safe precompiled PCRE pattern or equivalent timeout mechanism can prevent catastrophic backtracking.
material_risks: A globally blocked false positive could immediately disrupt traffic for many customers before the log-mode signal is detected.
A complex regex could cause pathological backtracking, raising request latency and exhausting CPU across edge proxies.
Delayed or partial Quicksilver propagation could leave some PoPs exposed or produce inconsistent enforcement.
Ten minutes of log mode leaves the newly disclosed attack unblocked during the observation period.
Aggregate match volume may conceal a severe false positive affecting a small customer or a concentrated real attack.
result.better_alternative: Use a risk-tiered expedited rollout: immediately block narrowly scoped, high-confidence exploit signatures, while logging broad rules and selectively canary-blocking them by PoP. Promote broad rules using production health and false-positive thresholds, rather than making a single global decision based only on aggregate match volume.

falsification_probe.description: Run the exact candidate regexes through the production PCRE engine against a representative peak-traffic trace containing sampled benign requests and all CI attack payloads, comparing shadow evaluation with the rules disabled.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if even a small candidate set causes backtracking or exceeds the proxy's allocated CPU/p99 latency budget, or if observed benign matches indicate a plausible customer-wide false positive; acceptable overhead and expected-only attack matches support the rollout.

result.recommendation: Keep the expedited global log-to-block model, but require a versioned atomic bundle, explicit benign-regression and PCRE complexity budgets, and automated promotion based on block volume, 5xx rate, latency, and CPU—not match volume alone. Preserve the previous bundle for immediate rollback, and define who can terminate or reverse the release; add a brief 1% block canary only if it still meets the one-hour objective.
critical_assumptions: A globally activated log-mode rule is propagated atomically and consistently within minutes.
Ten minutes of telemetry is timely and representative enough to expose false positives and operational regressions.
The CI suite includes benign requests in addition to attack payloads and runs before expedited activation.
Rule compilation and matching have enforced CPU, memory, and worst-case backtracking limits.
Block-mode changes can be rolled back globally within minutes without waiting for another configuration deployment.
material_risks: A high-cost PCRE consumes substantial proxy CPU in log mode before match-count monitoring detects degradation.
A benign traffic pattern absent from CI causes a global false-positive outage when block mode begins.
Match volume alone can remain normal while latency, 5xx responses, or regional traffic distributions deteriorate.
A non-atomic Quicksilver update can produce mixed rule versions or activate block mode before every proxy has validated the bundle.
Telemetry delay or concurrent updates can cause unsafe promotion or rollback to an unintended bundle.
result.better_alternative: Use the proposed global log window as the emergency safety gate, but combine it with deterministic pre-activation limits and automated multi-signal promotion: global log for 5–10 minutes, immediate rollback on any safety threshold breach, then block at 1% and 100% if latency and traffic permit. This is safer than relying on a fixed ten-minute timer while remaining within the disclosure-hour target.

falsification_probe.description: Replay a representative benign and adversarial request corpus through the candidate rule in log mode on a production-like proxy at measured peak request rate, comparing CPU and p99 latency with the rule disabled.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The design is viable only if worst-case evaluation stays within an agreed CPU and latency budget and no unbounded backtracking occurs; materially higher p99 latency, CPU saturation, or pathological evaluation time falsifies the claim that log mode is a safe universal first stage.

result.recommendation: Keep the expedited Quicksilver rollout, but do not make global blocking conditional only on aggregate match volume. Require bounded PCRE evaluation (complexity limits and a per-rule CPU/time budget), production-like load validation, and an automated rollback based on proxy latency, error rate, and false-positive indicators. Use a short 1% blocking canary with monitoring before global blocking, and aggregate or sample log-mode matches rather than performing unbounded per-request logging; this can still complete within the one-hour objective.
critical_assumptions: The CI corpus and benign-request set provide sufficiently representative coverage for newly disclosed attacks.
Quicksilver propagation and rule activation are atomic and fail-safe across all proxies and regions.
The WAF engine can enforce per-rule evaluation limits and disable a rule without taking down the proxy.
There is sufficient CPU headroom to evaluate the new rule on every request during log mode.
A reliable, low-latency signal exists for distinguishing attack matches from false positives.
material_risks: A catastrophic-backtracking or otherwise pathological regex could consume proxy CPU, increase request latency, or cause an outage even when it does not block requests.
A false-positive rule could block legitimate customer traffic globally after only ten minutes of insufficiently targeted monitoring.
Attackers could deliberately generate high match volume, making log mode itself expensive or obscuring benign false positives.
Inconsistent Quicksilver updates could leave some machines blocking while others only log, complicating incident response.
CI payload coverage may miss the disclosed exploit variant, allowing the rule to be published without detecting the actual attack.

falsification_probe.description: Run a production-like peak-load benchmark with the candidate rule enabled in log mode on the proxy, comparing CPU utilization, p95/p99 latency, request errors, and match-processing cost against the same workload without the rule.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if log-mode evaluation materially reduces available CPU or violates the proxy's latency/error SLOs, or if match volume causes unsafe logging overhead; negligible overhead and stable latency support proceeding with the expedited path.

result.recommendation: Retain the expedited Quicksilver path, but add worst-case CPU/latency limits, verify atomic and authenticated version activation, and provide an independently tested kill switch before blocking globally. Use representative canaries and centralized attack/false-positive telemetry, and deploy a minimal containment rule immediately while the complete signature is validated.
critical_assumptions: CI payload-corpus coverage is sufficient to detect harmful rules and known attack variants.
Quicksilver can activate one version atomically and consistently across every PoP within the response window.
The candidate rule has bounded worst-case CPU and regex-backtracking behavior under peak load.
Ten minutes of global log-mode telemetry is sufficient to expose false positives and attack misses.
A tested rollback or kill switch can remove the rule globally within minutes without proxy restart.
material_risks: A catastrophically expensive regex could exhaust CPU across all proxies before log mode detects it.
A false positive could then block legitimate traffic globally when the rule changes to block mode.
A partial or delayed rollout could leave inconsistent protection despite a nominally immediate publish.
Encoding, parser, or protocol variants may pass the corpus and remain unblocked.
Compilation, cache invalidation, or activation performed on the request path could itself cause an outage.
result.better_alternative: Publish a minimal, narrowly scoped containment rule immediately, then validate and activate the full signature through corpus, performance, representative canary, atomic-version, and automated rollback gates within the hour.

falsification_probe.description: Benchmark the exact candidate rule against worst-case and representative payloads at peak concurrency, including any CI-corpus edge cases, while measuring proxy CPU and request latency.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if the rule can exceed the predefined CPU or latency budget, show superlinear backtracking, or miss disclosed exploit variants; safe bounded behavior supports proceeding with the additional rollout controls.

result.recommendation: Retain immediate Quicksilver propagation, but do not make a global block decision solely from a 10-minute log window. Require explicit false-positive and performance gates, use a very short global or representative canary in log mode, and define an automatic rollback/kill switch based on error rate, latency, CPU, and match-volume anomalies. Ramp blocking across PoPs or traffic percentages within the hour, with an emergency mechanism independent of the normal rollout pipeline.
critical_assumptions: CI payload coverage predicts production behavior for a newly disclosed attack.
The new regex cannot cause pathological backtracking or excessive evaluation cost on attacker-controlled input.
Quicksilver propagation is sufficiently fast and atomic across all PoPs to meet the one-hour objective.
A 10-minute log interval provides statistically and operationally meaningful visibility into false positives and match volume.
The WAF has reliable real-time telemetry and a tested mechanism to disable or roll back a bad rule.
material_risks: A catastrophic or merely expensive regex could consume the proxy CPU shared with TLS and HTTP handling, causing latency, timeouts, or outages across customer traffic.
The rule may block legitimate requests that were absent from the benign CI corpus, creating a global availability or business-impact incident.
A low or misleading match volume can be caused by logging failures, sampling, traffic-shape differences, or an incomplete attack signature, leading to premature blocking.
A globally propagated bad rule cannot be recalled quickly enough, and a 10-minute observation window may be too short to observe rare benign traffic.
Simultaneous deployment of many rules may create aggregate CPU or evaluation-budget overruns even when each rule passes isolated tests.

falsification_probe.description: Replay the rule against a representative production request corpus, including benign traffic and adversarial regex inputs, at projected peak concurrency, and compare proxy CPU utilization and request latency with the rule disabled.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if the rule causes unacceptable CPU growth, latency, timeouts, or evaluation-budget exhaustion under realistic traffic; otherwise this validates only the performance prerequisite, not the safety of global blocking.

result.recommendation: Retain immediate global shadow deployment, but require hard rule evaluation budgets, payload-variant verification, representative canary enforcement, automated health/false-positive gates, and a tested global kill switch before promotion. Treat ten minutes as a minimum evidence window rather than an automatic promotion timer, and prioritize proven high-confidence signatures for blocking within minutes.
critical_assumptions: CI’s benign corpus represents production traffic and input encodings closely enough to prevent broad false positives.
Quicksilver can activate and later roll back rules globally within minutes with bounded version skew.
The ten-minute log period provides sufficiently complete, timely, representative match and latency telemetry.
New rules have bounded worst-case PCRE execution under concurrent peak load.
A coherent log-to-block transition and emergency rollback mechanism already exists or will be added.
material_risks: A pathological PCRE or high-match-volume rule consumes proxy CPU and degrades TLS and HTTP service for every customer at that PoP.
The rule logs rather than blocks during the initial window, or blocks before all machines are ready, leaving material exposure to the disclosed attack.
Rare benign requests absent from CI are blocked after a superficially normal ten-minute match-volume result.
Quicksilver skew or a failed transition produces partial protection or inconsistent enforcement for longer than the objective permits.
The signature matches the test payload but misses common encodings, alternate syntaxes, or actual exploit variants.
result.better_alternative: Use a risk-tiered emergency pipeline: shadow deploy globally, enforce narrowly scoped high-confidence signatures immediately or after very short canaries, and delay uncertain or CPU-heavy rules until broader validation. Promote only after automated checks on attack matches, benign match deltas, evaluation time, proxy saturation, and rollout completeness, with automatic global rollback.

falsification_probe.description: Run every eligible emergency rule in the existing CI harness against its payload variants, the benign corpus, and generated pathological inputs under representative peak concurrency, reporting incremental per-request evaluation time and worst-case completion time.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The design is falsified if any rule that would pass the current CI corpus exceeds the documented per-request CPU/time budget, can exhibit unbounded backtracking, or blocks any benign sample. Results showing bounded cost and zero benign matches would support the shadow-to-block mechanism, though production representativeness and rollout controls would still need validation.

result.recommendation: Keep the expedited, infrastructure-based rollout, but do not treat a 10-minute log-only period as sufficient safety validation. Require adversarial regex complexity and performance tests before publication, enforce signed/versioned atomic bundles and per-rule rollback, and use explicit CPU, latency, and false-positive thresholds before global blocking; add a narrowly scoped emergency containment rule when the final signature is not immediately safe.
critical_assumptions: Quicksilver can atomically publish a consistent, signed rule bundle to every machine and transition modes within the target hour.
The WAF evaluator supports rule-level log/block transitions and rollback without restarting proxies.
A rule passing the existing CI corpus has acceptable worst-case PCRE behavior on malformed and adversarial inputs.
Near-real-time match counts and request health metrics are available and trustworthy during the 10-minute window.
Log-mode evaluation has approximately the same CPU cost as block-mode evaluation.
material_risks: Catastrophic regex backtracking can exhaust proxy CPU even while the rule is only logging, affecting all customer traffic.
A low match count can be caused by a faulty, narrowly scoped, or traffic-dependent rule and therefore does not establish safety.
A false positive discovered after the global block transition can affect every PoP simultaneously.
Inconsistent bundle versions or mode transitions can create temporary unprotected gaps or conflicting behavior.
A compromised release credential or control plane could inject a globally evaluated denial rule.
result.better_alternative: Use a hybrid release: deploy a narrowly scoped temporary deny policy immediately where appropriate, then publish the precise rule globally in log mode for 1–5 minutes with automated performance and false-positive gates, followed by rapid promotion and one-click per-rule rollback. This preserves sub-hour protection while reducing reliance on a single noisy observation window.

falsification_probe.description: Replay the candidate rule and a representative/adversarial benign corpus through the actual WAF evaluator on a production-equivalent proxy, including encoded, truncated, and pathological inputs, while measuring CPU, p95/p99 latency, and evaluation count.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if any input causes superlinear evaluation, CPU saturation, or unacceptable proxy latency; also falsified if log-mode overhead is materially lower than block-mode overhead.

result.recommendation: Retain expedited propagation, but replace the unconditional 10-minute global log window with a compressed, observable rollout: begin in log mode, promote through small canaries, and reach global block within the one-hour objective only if false-positive and latency thresholds remain healthy. Require per-rule automatic rollback, confirm propagation completeness, and enforce regex complexity, evaluation-time, and CPU-budget limits before activation.
critical_assumptions: Quicksilver propagation and activation are atomic enough that no machine remains indefinitely on the old rule version.
Match counts can be attributed to each rule and monitored with sufficiently low latency to trigger rollback.
A ten-minute observation period contains traffic representative enough to expose likely false positives.
Candidate PCREs cannot cause pathological backtracking or materially increase peak CPU.

result.recommendation: Keep the idempotency-key table and fingerprint checks, but move processor work off POST through a transactional outbox and return 202 with a stable payment/status URL. result.recommendation: Keep scoped idempotency records and a stable processor token, but make payment creation asynchronous so the API can durably accept a command and return within the 1 s p99 target. On duplicate keys, wait briefly for a terminal result and then return 202 with a status URL rather than an immediate 409; reserve 409 for an actual in-progress conflict only if clients explicitly poll or retry it.
critical_assumptions: The processor guarantees that reuse of the same token, including concurrent requests and requests after client timeouts, produces at most one charge for at least the full retry window.
Token derivation is deterministic, collision-free across accounts or tenants, accepted by the processor, and does not expose a reusable client key.
The idempotency record and its state transitions are durably committed before any processor call that could charge.
All retries preserve the same authenticated account_id and canonical request fingerprint.
Returning 409 for unfinished duplicates will not cause clients to abandon the logical payment or violate the intended retry protocol.

result.recommendation: Keep the idempotency-table and stable processor-token design, but specify atomic key claiming, transaction boundaries, and recovery for a crash or timeout after sending the processor request. Define whether 409 is retryable, ensure processor tokens and local records remain valid for the entire client retry window, and add reconciliation or a status-query path when the processor outcome is unknown.
critical_assumptions: The processor idempotency token is durable, uniquely scoped to the intended charge, and honored for retries after service failure.
The PostgreSQL uniqueness constraint and payment/processor state transitions can be made atomic under concurrent requests and process crashes.
A deterministic token derived from (account_id, key) is accepted by the processor without collision or sensitive-data leakage.
Clients preserve and reuse the same key for the entire logical payment, including retries after 409 or timeout responses.
The 24-hour local retention period is at least as long as the processor's idempotency retention and all plausible client retry delays.

Returning 409 without an explicit retry contract can cause clients to stop retrying or generate a new key, producing inconsistent behavior.
Records expiring before delayed retries or before processor reconciliation can reopen duplicate-processing windows.

The authenticated account ID and canonical request fields are available before attempting the processor call.
A PostgreSQL outbox/worker can claim jobs durably and recover them after process failure.

A crash can leave the payment permanently in progress because the proposal does not specify a durable worker or recovery query to complete the processor call.
Synchronous processor latency is on the POST path, so p99 below 1 s is not established and may be infeasible.
Expiring keys after 24 hours can permit a late retry to create a new charge, especially if processor token retention is longer.
Deriving a processor token solely from an unnamespaced client key can cause collisions across accounts or tenants unless the derivation is globally unique and stable.

falsification_probe.description: Run an integration test against the processor: issue a charge with a token, simulate a lost response, then retry the same token from a separate process while inspecting processor-side charge identifiers.

Scope that token by account and service, persist the token itself rather than relying on a reversible derivation, and verify the processor retains idempotency tokens for at least the full 24-hour replay window.

Processor idempotency-token retention is at least 24 hours.
Tokens are scoped by merchant/account, or the derivation includes a collision-resistant account and service identifier.
A database transaction can atomically claim a key using an expiring lease.
The request fingerprint is computed over a stable canonical representation of every payment-affecting field.

Deriving the processor token solely from the client key can collide across accounts or merchant scopes.

falsification_probe.description: Run an integration test that kills the service after the processor accepts the request but before the final response is stored, waits until the database lease expires, and retries the same request and key.

result.recommendation: Persist an explicit pending/unknown payment state before the processor call and add durable recovery for crashes between the processor request, response, and local state update; an in-progress row must not remain stranded forever. Benchmark the synchronous path against the sub-1-second p99 requirement, and align local key retention with the client retry window and processor idempotency retention period; use an asynchronous outbox/worker if the benchmark fails.
critical_assumptions: Processor token derivation includes account or payment identity, preventing cross-account collisions when clients reuse a key.
The processor retains idempotency results for at least as long as clients may retry and at least as long as local records are retained.

The key row is durably committed before any processor request, and recovery can distinguish never-sent from unknown-outcome calls.
All clients preserve the same key with exponential backoff and jitter until a terminal response is received.

Expiring local keys after 24 hours permits a late retry to initiate a second charge unless the processor still suppresses it or a durable payment identity remains.
A processor token derived only from the client key can collide across accounts and reject or confuse unrelated payments.
Synchronous processor latency may violate the sub-1-second creation p99.
Returning only 409 while processing may induce clients with finite retry policies to abandon and independently initiate payment.

result.recommendation: Persist the idempotency reservation transactionally before calling the processor, and derive a stable processor token from a merchant/account namespace plus the key—not from the key alone. Make local retention at least as long as processor token retention, define expiry behavior explicitly, and return 503 with Retry-After while work is in progress so existing clients actually retry. falsification_probe.description: Run one integration test with two authenticated accounts sending the same Idempotency-Key but different amounts, using a processor stub or sandbox whose token scope is the merchant.

result.recommendation: Retain the local idempotency ledger and processor token, but define an explicit state machine with atomic pre-call persistence, ownership/leases, and processor-status reconciliation after crashes; an indefinitely abandoned processing row must not merely return 409. To reliably meet p99 below 1 second, durably accept the payment and process the processor call asynchronously, returning a stable acceptance response that retries replay. Specify canonical fingerprinting, processor/account token scoping, retry semantics for 409, and coordinated key/token expiry.
critical_assumptions: The processor deduplicates concurrent and sequential requests for the same token and exposes a way to determine the original request's outcome.
Processor token retention is at least as long as the API replay window, including delayed retries after crashes.
The service atomically persists and owns the processing record before making the processor call.
Clients preserve one key for the entire logical payment and can interpret or poll an asynchronous acceptance response.
A derived token is unique within the processor's actual merchant/account scope, not merely within this service's account_id scope.

falsification_probe.description: In the processor sandbox, submit the same payment twice concurrently with the exact same scoped token, including one simulated client disconnect after processor acceptance, then query or retry that token.

Any second charge, a permanently unknown result, or rejection of the reused token would falsify the proposal's safety assumptions and require replacement of its recovery design.

Validate the exact claim query and projected load with EXPLAIN and a benchmark; revisit the 1,000 jobs/s threshold only after measuring database saturation, job duration, and operational requirements.

Every handler is safe under duplicate execution, including emails and webhooks.

The pending index matches the actual queue predicate and ordering, including status and run_at conditions.
The database has enough connection, I/O, WAL, and lock capacity at the forecast peak and during batch cleanup.

Deleting completed jobs after seven days can remove audit, debugging, or deduplication history required by handlers or operations.

Validate that workers hold the row lock through successful processing or use a recoverable lease/stale-job mechanism, and require idempotency for external side effects so retries cannot cause harmful duplicate emails, PDFs, or webhooks.
critical_assumptions: Workers either process the job while holding the row lock in the business transaction or have a reliable stale-job recovery mechanism.
Job rows are durably committed in PostgreSQL and are not deleted before successful completion or an explicitly safe retention period.
External side effects are idempotent or protected against duplicate delivery.
The proposed indexes match the actual queue-selection predicates and failed-job queries.

A transiently healthy subscriber may acknowledge or attempt processing immediately before crashing, with no broker-side redelivery guarantee.

Treating Redis cache and rate-limit pressure as isolated becomes unsafe once job loss or restart pressure is coupled to those services.

Rollback remains safe after new-manager enforcement has affected replicated user-ID writes.
material_risks: Incomplete historical usage reconstruction could immediately overgrant or falsely reject users.
Enabling automatic reductions without shadow comparison could mishandle sustained-underuse reductions and cause user-visible quota changes.
Semantic differences in overrides, exemptions, or grace-period handling could produce incorrect enforcement.
Deregistering legacy before parity is demonstrated removes the authoritative fallback and makes rollback incomplete.
Moving user-ID in a general wave without regional-failover testing could cause inconsistent accepts, rejects, or split-brain enforcement.
result.better_alternative: Use a shadow migration with legacy remaining authoritative, compare replicated usage and quota decisions against it, and progressively transfer enforcement through controlled canaries; place user-ID last with explicit failover and automated rollback tests.

falsification_probe.description: Select one low-risk service and replay a full grace period of production-like usage through both managers, including an override, an exemption, and a sustained-underuse reduction, then diff every decision and final allocation.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any missing usage, decision mismatch, or allocation discrepancy falsifies the claim that registration plus allocation copying is sufficient for safe cutover; exact parity supports proceeding only through shadow and gated rollout.

result.recommendation: Keep the wave-based migration, but initially disable automatic quota reductions or add a per-service reduction freeze while validating parity and rollback behavior. Migrate the user-ID service only after testing replicated writes, reporting lag, and enforcement at the allocation boundary; retain legacy registration and a tested rollback path until each wave is proven stable.
critical_assumptions: The new manager can copy allocations without changing quota semantics or effective capacity.
Both managers can remain registered during migration, or equivalent shadow enforcement and rollback are available.
Reported usage is sufficiently complete, timely, and comparable across regions and services.
Automatic reductions cannot cause a service's legitimate burst usage to exceed its allocation.
Deregistering from the legacy manager does not remove an independent enforcement path or monitoring dependency.
material_risks: Automatic reductions may reject writes for the user-ID service, including login/account operations, violating the no-user-visible-impact requirement.
Usage-reporting lag or regional replication inconsistency could make the new manager undercount usage and permit writes beyond the intended quota, or overcount and reject valid writes.
Migrating the user-ID database's enforcement path without a tested rollback could interrupt authentication globally.
A copied allocation may not represent current effective limits, causing an immediate quota breach during cutover.
Deregistration before parity is established could eliminate the only known-good enforcement or usage signal.
result.better_alternative: Use a staged shadow migration: dual-register services, mirror and compare usage and enforcement decisions while preserving legacy behavior, keep allocations frozen and reductions disabled, then canary enforcement and rollback before making the new manager authoritative. Handle user-ID separately with multi-region write-failure and authentication tests.

falsification_probe.description: Inspect the new quota system's configuration/API and run a non-production simulation for one canary service whose reported usage stays below allocation, followed by a burst that reaches the current allocation.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the allocation is reduced during the grace period or the burst is rejected because of the reduction, the proposed 'no user-visible impact' assumption is falsified; if reductions can be disabled and enforcement is unchanged, the mitigation is viable.

result.recommendation: Retain the wave migration, but add shadow-mode validation and explicitly freeze automatic reduction for user-ID during migration and until its reports and enforcement behavior are proven across regions. Before deregistration, compare both systems’ usage and decisions at peak load, and retain a tested rollback path until the new system meets availability and write-rejection targets.
critical_assumptions: The new system can disable automatic reduction for user-ID without affecting other services.
Usage reports are complete, sufficiently current, and consistent across regions.
Legacy and new systems use equivalent allocation, accounting, grace-period, and enforcement semantics.
Registration changes can be coordinated so the service is never simultaneously unenrolled or subject to conflicting enforcement.
The new manager can meet user-ID’s latency, availability, and multi-region consistency requirements.
material_risks: A delayed or understated usage report can cause the new system to reject valid user-ID database writes across regions.
Automatic reduction can lower user-ID allocation below demand before the grace-period buffer accounts for actual reporting lag.
A mismatch in quota semantics can unexpectedly enforce a lower effective limit than the legacy manager.
Deregistering from legacy before validating the new path removes the ability to roll back safely.
Inconsistent or missing regional data can produce different enforcement outcomes, causing partial or intermittent login-account write failures.
result.better_alternative: Migrate noncritical services first in shadow mode, then migrate user-ID with automatic reductions disabled and a deliberately padded, fixed allocation. Dual-report and compare usage and decisions under peak multi-region load, retain legacy fallback for a defined observation period, and only then deregister legacy; enable automatic reductions later once operational evidence supports it.

falsification_probe.description: Run user-ID in dual-reporting shadow mode for a representative peak-load period, including all regions, and compare the legacy and new systems’ usage totals, allocation values, and would-reject decisions; also measure report age and cross-region convergence.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal would be falsified if reports are materially stale or region-inconsistent, semantics differ, or the new system would reject writes that the legacy system accepts under the copied allocation.

result.recommendation: Keep the wave structure and placing user-ID later, but do not deregister any service until the new system has shadow-evaluated real usage and demonstrated parity with the legacy decision for an agreed observation period. Start automatic reductions in non-enforcing or conservatively bounded mode, and add explicit completeness, cross-region, rollback, and emergency-bypass gates; dashboards alone are insufficient.
critical_assumptions: Copying the current allocation preserves the legacy system's units, scope, grace-period semantics, and enforcement behavior.
New-system usage reports are complete, timely, deduplicated, and consistent across regions before legacy enforcement is removed.
Automatic allocation reductions cannot produce a harmful false reduction or reduce resilience below required peaks during the grace period.
Each wave can be rolled back or temporarily bypassed without losing authoritative quota enforcement, especially for replicated user-ID writes.
A wave's services and policies are fully inventoried, with no legacy-only exceptions or split registrations.
material_risks: A semantic mismatch or incorrect allocation translation could reject valid user-ID writes and impair login globally.
Stale, missing, duplicated, or regionally inconsistent reports could trigger enforcement or reduction against incorrect usage.
The proposal has no pre-enforcement comparison, so discrepancies are discovered while users are exposed rather than during shadow operation.
The observation that a grace period is long does not protect against a sharp usage increase, report outage, replication event, or misconfigured reduction policy.
Wave rollback may restore legacy registration only after data or policy diverges, leaving no safe immediate enforcement path.
result.better_alternative: Use shadow-first wave migration: register a cohort without making the new system authoritative, compare historical and live usage, effective allocations, grace-period transitions, and would-be write decisions against the legacy manager, and require predefined parity thresholds. Then enforce on a small cohort, retain tested rollback or bypass controls through the observation period, and enable automatic reduction only after telemetry completeness and reduction behavior are validated; migrate user-ID with conservative limits and cross-region failure testing.

falsification_probe.description: Run the new quota engine in non-enforcing mode for one representative cohort, replay available historical reports, and compare its effective allocation, reduction schedule, and enforcement decisions with the legacy manager over a period covering grace-period transitions.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any unexplained decision mismatch, missing/late report, cross-region discrepancy, or materially different reduction schedule falsifies copy-and-deregister as a safe default; exact agreement across representative cases supports proceeding with the modified gates.

result.recommendation: Keep the wave migration, but do not enable automatic quota reduction for the user-ID service until a global peak-load test demonstrates that its allocation has sufficient headroom for the entire reduction and regional replication delay window. Make manager cutover explicit and reversible to avoid overlapping enforcement or an enforcement gap, and retain a protected allocation and tested rollback path for user-ID throughout migration.
critical_assumptions: Copied allocations include enough capacity for user-ID growth and traffic spikes.
Usage reports are accurate, timely, and consistent across regions.
Quota decisions propagate to every database replica before writes are evaluated.
Registration and deregistration cannot create dual authority or an enforcement gap.
The stated grace period includes all propagation, scheduling, and regional failover delays.
material_risks: Automatic reduction could cause user-ID database writes to be rejected during normal or peak login traffic.
A stale or region-specific usage report could trigger an unsafe quota reduction.
Concurrent registration in both managers could produce conflicting enforcement decisions.
A gap during deregistration could leave user-ID writes without quota enforcement.
Insufficient regional consistency could allow the global allocation to be exceeded before enforcement converges.
result.better_alternative: Migrate noncritical services in waves, but place user-ID in shadow mode first and use a fixed, protected allocation for its initial cutover. Enable automatic reduction only after production-scale testing across regions establishes safe headroom, then increase usage or allocation alerts before each reduction.

falsification_probe.description: Run a production-scale user-ID write test against the new system using current and forecast peak traffic, exercising all regional replicas with realistic propagation delay and one failover.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any legitimate account create or update is rejected, any replica observes a different enforcement state, or projected usage approaches the copied allocation before the earliest possible reduction confirms the proposal is unsafe as written.

result.recommendation: Keep the wave-based migration, but run the new manager in shadow/dual-report mode and compare usage, allocations, grace-period boundaries, and rejection decisions before making it authoritative. Cut over services and regions incrementally behind an enforcement flag, with an explicit rollback procedure that freezes or synchronizes allocation state; enable automatic reduction only after parity, load, replication-lag, and failover testing. Do not deregister the legacy manager until a bounded observation period, telemetry/audit validation, and incident rollback procedures are complete.
critical_assumptions: Copying the current allocation is sufficient to preserve authorization state and does not lose pending reductions or grace-period metadata.
The grace period reliably delays automatic allocation changes without delaying quota enforcement or creating a large rejection window.
The new manager can make authoritative quota decisions synchronously for user-ID writes, including during replication lag and regional failover.
Legacy and new managers produce equivalent decisions for production usage, allocation reductions, and grace-period edge cases.
A rollback can preserve or reconstruct the last authoritative allocation state without inconsistent authorization.
material_risks: Directly deregistering the legacy manager after copying allocations can reject legitimate user-ID database writes because of timing, semantic, or propagation differences.
Enabling automatic reduction universally can unexpectedly shrink allocations or trigger false rejections before parity and grace-period behavior are validated.
Cross-region failover could use stale or divergent quota state and block replicated writes or allow over-quota operations.
Fallback after the new manager has reclaimed allocations could make legacy and new authorization states inconsistent.
Usage and allocation dashboards alone may not provide decision-level auditability, discrepancy detection, or proof that rollback and incident procedures work.
result.better_alternative: Use a staged shadow-and-cutover design: mirror reports and allocations while legacy remains authoritative, establish discrepancy thresholds and an end date, then migrate low-risk services and user-ID by region behind a reversible enforcement flag. Preserve allocation state during rollback and retire legacy only after synchronous-write, concurrent-request, replication-lag, failover, telemetry, and operational-readiness tests pass.

falsification_probe.description: Replay a production-representative history of usage and allocation changes through both managers, including grace-period boundaries and allocation reductions, and compare their synchronous allow/reject decisions.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any material decision mismatch, especially a new-manager rejection where legacy allows a valid write or a reduction occurring before the intended grace-period boundary, falsifies the claimed safe direct cutover.

result.recommendation: Keep the wave migration, but place the user-ID service in a dedicated early canary with dual reporting and shadow enforcement, and do not deregister the legacy manager until multi-region validation and rollback are proven. Initially disable automatic reductions or set an explicit allocation floor for the user-ID service, then enable reductions only after monitoring shows accurate usage, expected headroom, and safe behavior under replication and failover. Keep the legacy manager available through the quarter until each service has completed an observation period and an independently tested rollback.
critical_assumptions: The new quota manager can accurately receive and attribute user-ID usage from every region without a reporting gap during handoff.
Allocation values and quota semantics are identical between the legacy and new managers, or any differences have been reconciled.
The user-ID database has enough write and authentication headroom for delayed, stale, or inconsistent usage data.
Automatic quota reduction can be delayed, overridden, or given a safe minimum allocation for at least the user-ID service.
A tested rollback can restore legacy enforcement without losing writes or creating divergent quota state.

Because the database replicates writes across regions, one region's stale or excessive usage report could trigger quota rejection in another region and produce global user-visible impact.

Deregistering the legacy manager before proving rollback would remove the only known safe enforcement path and make recovery dependent on the new system's state.
A copied allocation may not account for migration traffic, failover, backlog, or growth, leaving insufficient capacity despite apparently matching configuration.
result.better_alternative: Migrate the user-ID service first under dual reporting and shadow evaluation, with reductions disabled and both managers receiving data. Compare decisions across regions, test quota rejection and recovery under simulated failover and stale telemetry, then perform a canary handoff with immediate rollback; migrate the remaining services in waves and enable reductions gradually only after verified headroom and stable telemetry.

falsification_probe.description: In a staging replica of the user-ID database, verify whether the new manager supports a per-service hold on automatic allocation reduction; if it does, lower the simulated allocation below current usage and exercise writes and logins in each region.

result.recommendation: Keep the wave-based direction, but add a shadow/validation phase that compares legacy and new usage and quota decisions before each enforcement cutover. Migrate user-ID with an explicitly tested, reversible write-admission procedure, and initially disable automatic reduction for it or prove that grace-period and reporting guarantees are safe. Confirm that allocation copies include all overrides and policies, and remove legacy only after a dependency check and bounded rollback window.
critical_assumptions: The new system can receive complete, consistent, and timely usage reports from every region before it becomes authoritative.
Switching a service's registration also switches the enforcement path atomically, or the proposal provides an equivalent mechanism preventing split or stale decisions.
Allocation copies preserve all service-specific overrides, reservations, exemptions, and policy settings.
The automatic-reduction grace period is safe under delayed reporting, outages, seasonal usage, and regional replication lag.
A reversible user-ID enforcement cutover can be performed without causing inconsistent replicated writes or user-visible login failures.

User-ID quota enforcement errors can block database writes during login and account operations, and regional replication may produce inconsistent cross-region outcomes.
A copied allocation may differ from the effective legacy allocation, immediately tightening or loosening user-ID storage admission.
Enabling automatic reductions for user-ID during telemetry gaps or abnormal low-usage periods could cause genuine capacity denials.
Deregistering services too early may leave operational consumers dependent on the legacy manager, while shutting it down without a tested rollback could eliminate recovery options.
result.better_alternative: Use shadow-and-validate migration: run the new manager in observation-only mode using the same usage reports, compare its projected decisions with legacy behavior, then perform independently reversible enforcement cutovers. For user-ID, use a dedicated readiness gate, regional canary or controlled validation, conservative allocation floors, and tested fail-open/fail-closed and rollback behavior before enabling reductions.

falsification_probe.description: Replay a representative production history of user-ID usage, allocation changes, reporting delays, and regional lag through the proposed registration/cutover and automatic-reduction sequence, then compare the new manager's admission decisions with the legacy manager's actual decisions.

result.recommendation: Keep wave-based migration and user-ID-last, but add shadow-mode decision comparison, explicit exit criteria per wave, and independently reversible cutover controls. Do not enable automatic quota reduction on the first authoritative cutovers: validate reporting completeness and grace-period behavior first, then enable it service by service; dashboards alone are not safety controls.
critical_assumptions: Copying an allocation preserves its effective value, unit, and reset/grace-period semantics in the new system.
Deregistering a service immediately redirects all usage reports and enforcement checks to only the new manager.
Usage reporting is complete and timely enough that automatic reduction cannot mistake missing telemetry for low usage.
The new manager's decisions are consistent across regions before user-ID begins relying on them.
Service owners can detect and reverse a bad cutover before user-ID writes are affected.

Deregistration can create an enforcement gap if old and new registrations do not update atomically.

result.better_alternative: Use a staged strangler design: run the new manager in shadow mode, compare every prospective accept/reject and allocation-reduction decision with the current authority, and promote one low-risk service at a time behind reversible flags. Keep user-ID shadowed through the final quarter and cut it over only after regional lag, failover, and partition tests; preserve a time-boxed rollback path before shutting down legacy.

falsification_probe.description: Replay historical and synthetic low-usage, missing-report, stale-report, threshold-crossing, and grace-period-boundary events through both managers and compare accept/reject and allocation-reduction decisions.

result.recommendation: Keep the phased migration, but exempt the user-ID service from automatic quota reduction or configure a conservative floor based on measured peak usage, replication lag, and operational growth. Validate this behavior under write load before cutover, and retain legacy reporting or an equivalent rapid rollback path until the new system is proven stable.
critical_assumptions: The new quota system supports a per-service exemption, fixed floor, or equivalent override for automatic reduction.
Reported user-ID usage includes all distributed writes and is sufficiently current across regions.
Current allocations have enough headroom for normal peaks and cross-region replication lag.
An allocation reduction can be detected and reversed before production writes are rejected.

Deregistering from the legacy manager without a tested rollback may remove the recovery path needed during regional instability.

result.recommendation: Add a shadow-and-compare phase before each cohort moves, using historical and live near-threshold traffic to verify usage semantics, allocation/grace behavior, and regional consistency. Keep a time-bounded legacy fallback with explicit rollback criteria, and initially disable automatic reductions or prove their parity before enabling them; dashboards alone are insufficient validation.
critical_assumptions: Legacy and new usage reports have identical units, scope, deduplication, and timestamp semantics.
Copying current allocations also preserves grace-period and delayed/missing-report behavior.
Services can switch registration and enforcement paths at runtime and safely recover from quota-manager outages.
Regional replication and failover enforce consistent quota decisions.
Automatic reductions cannot reject legitimate writes before the grace period provides safe rollback time.

Semantic reporting differences create false quota exceedances or allow excess storage.
Replication lag or regional conflicts cause inconsistent write acceptance and account-data divergence.
An omitted service or lost connectivity leaves usage unmanaged while deregistered from the legacy manager.
Enabling automatic reductions during migration compounds allocation mismatches and removes the rollback safety margin.

Retain a controlled legacy fallback until parity, resilience, audit, and rollback exit criteria pass.

falsification_probe.description: Replay historical and recent live user-ID usage, including near-threshold, delayed, missing, and out-of-order reports, through both managers in shadow mode and compare every allocation and enforcement decision by region.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: Any material unexplained decision mismatch, false rejection, regional divergence, or difference in grace and missing-report behavior would falsify the proposed wave cutover as currently specified.

result.recommendation: Add an explicit reconciliation and cutover protocol: pre-populate historical usage, disable automatic reductions until each service has established complete reporting with the new manager, and require warm-up plus health verification before deregistration. For user-ID, use conservative fixed allocations, cross-region enforcement testing, and an independently controlled rollback/kill switch; do not rely on the generic grace period as the sole safeguard.
critical_assumptions: Copying the current allocation also initializes enough historical usage data to prevent immediate automatic reduction.
Registration and deregistration cannot create an interval in which inconsistent quota decisions are enforced.
Usage-reporting completeness and freshness are comparable between the legacy and new systems.
The new manager's reduced allocation propagates consistently across all user-ID database regions.

During migration, the service might report to one manager while enforcement or stale usage data is obtained from the other, producing inconsistent accept/reject decisions.
The claimed grace period may begin before sufficient observations are collected, allowing an unproven allocation reduction.
Allocation copies may omit reserved, archival, replication, compaction, or growth requirements that the legacy manager included.
Deregistering the legacy manager without a tested rollback path could leave the service with no effective quota enforcement or make rollback unsafe.
result.better_alternative: Migrate noncritical services through a shadow period with dual reporting and decision comparison, followed by atomic enforcement cutover. Keep automatic reductions disabled until parity and forecasting thresholds are proven, then enable them first for low-risk services and only later for user-ID under fixed safety floors and regional write-failure tests.

falsification_probe.description: In staging, run user-ID with identical storage and replicated writes while the new manager is set just below current observed usage but above the proposed operational floor; then toggle manager registration during a write and inspect all regional write outcomes.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is unsafe if any region rejects a normal write, decisions differ between managers or regions, or registration transition changes enforcement before reporting is reconciled.

result.recommendation: Retain wave migration, but enable automatic reduction only after establishing a safety floor for user-ID and validating usage-decision parity between managers. Migrate user-ID last, switch enforcement atomically where possible, and require tested rollback before deregistering any service from the legacy manager.
critical_assumptions: The new system can accurately receive current user-ID allocations and usage reports from every region.

A new-system outage could block user-ID writes if enforcement fails closed.

Before each cutover, shadow or compare usage and enforcement decisions, then atomically transfer authority with rollback tested under concurrent regional writes.

falsification_probe.description: Query historical user-ID usage by region and compare maximum recent usage plus observed growth against its copied allocation through the full reduction grace period.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: If even peak-plus-projected-growth usage approaches the copied allocation during the grace period, the claim that weeks of buffer make universal automatic reduction safe is falsified and user-ID requires a floor or exemption.

result.recommendation: Keep streaming as the preferred direction, but do not enable it for all health subscriptions in one rollout. First verify the exact 1.10 configuration scope and client compatibility, then canary representative cohorts, measure CPU, network, update correctness, and reconnect behavior under realistic load, and expand only against explicit thresholds. Retain a tested configuration rollback and use query/watch tuning as a complementary control.
critical_assumptions: The deployed client and server versions support the same streaming protocol and configuration semantics.
`use_streaming_backend` is set at the correct agent/server scope and actually causes production health reads to use streaming rather than merely enabling an unused feature.
The 200-node staging workload is representative of production subscription breadth, result sizes, churn, and holiday concurrency.
Streaming preserves watch ordering, completeness, and freshness during reconnects and leader changes.
The rollout can be stopped or reverted quickly enough to prevent a fleet-wide failure.
material_risks: A mixed-version or mis-scoped rollout leaves blocking queries active or causes incompatible streaming behavior.
An all-at-once change can create a reconnect or subscription storm, increasing CPU, network, Raft pressure, and latency.
Incorrect streaming freshness or missed-event handling could leave services with stale dependency state or route traffic to unhealthy instances.
The staging CPU reduction may not scale linearly when every service subscribes simultaneously.
Because there is no discovery fallback, a streaming defect or partition could broadly disrupt service resolution.
result.better_alternative: Use a staged canary: begin with a bounded, diverse set of services and nodes, validate correctness and resource metrics during expected load, then expand by cohorts. Keep the existing blocking-query configuration available for immediate rollback, and add endpoint/watch coalescing or narrower subscriptions if streaming does not deliver the expected fleet-wide reduction.

falsification_probe.description: Run the proposed 200-node staging configuration under a production-representative subscription mix and concurrent holiday-level load, while comparing effective configuration and measuring server CPU, network bytes, streaming versus blocking-query counts, and watch freshness or missed updates.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if clients do not actually use streaming, or if streaming causes material missed/stale updates, a reconnect storm, or higher server CPU/network than the current blocking-query baseline at representative load; a reproducible, scalable CPU reduction with correct updates supports expansion.

result.recommendation: Retain streaming, but verify and configure `use_streaming_backend` in the scope required by Consul 1.10—particularly whether it is a server-side setting rather than only a client setting—and perform a production canary with explicit rollback thresholds. Progressively expand only after validating client compatibility, streaming-session errors, CPU, network, latency, and Raft health across servers and representative failure scenarios.
critical_assumptions: The installed client versions and service integrations support Consul 1.10 streaming correctly.
`use_streaming_backend` is being enabled in the configuration scope that actually activates the feature.
A mixed-version rolling upgrade and selective enablement are supported during deployment.
Streaming reduces load at 18,000-node production scale, not only in the 200-node staging environment.
Consul can safely recreate streaming sessions after server failure or leader election.

falsification_probe.expected_signal: If the option is server-scoped, the client-only proposal is incorrect; if the documented scope is client-side, no streaming sessions appear, or staging CPU/network do not improve materially, the proposed rollout is falsified.

result.recommendation: Keep the streaming direction, but replace the single fleet-wide rollout with a small representative canary followed by staged cohort expansion. Before expansion, verify semantic equivalence, freshness and ordering, reconnect/error behavior, fallback capacity, and end-to-end CPU, network, memory, Raft, and client resource impact; retain blocking-query fallback and define rollback thresholds.
critical_assumptions: All production client versions, libraries, platforms, and service implementations support Consul 1.10 streaming without changing dependency or health-data semantics.
The staging 200-node test represents production update rates, query patterns, reconnects, and failure behavior rather than only demonstrating a CPU reduction.
The five-server cluster has sufficient spare capacity for streaming, reconnects, and any temporary blocking-query fallback during rollback.
Streaming will not materially increase Raft commits, memory, network traffic, or client CPU in production.
A six-week canary and staged rollout can complete without rushing compatibility or operational validation.

Reconnect storms could overload the five voting servers or increase Raft and network load even while server CPU falls.
Rolling back or falling back to blocking queries could create a traffic surge and service-discovery disruption.
The observed 60% staging CPU reduction may not hold under production update rates, concurrency, or network and memory costs.
A single rollout provides little isolation or opportunity to detect service-specific failures before affecting all services.
result.better_alternative: Use a phased migration: canary a small representative set, measure correctness and end-to-end resource impact under load, then expand by service or node cohort while retaining blocking-query support and explicit rollback thresholds.

falsification_probe.description: Run one representative production-like load test in staging with both protocols, including health updates, client reconnects, and fallback, then compare semantic correctness and server, network, Raft, and client metrics.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The proposal is falsified if streaming changes health-data freshness, completeness, or ordering, increases errors or reconnect load, or fails to reduce end-to-end cost after accounting for network, memory, Raft, and client overhead; a clean result with sustained CPU savings supports staged expansion.

result.recommendation: Retain streaming, but do not enable it fleet-wide at once. Upgrade servers in a supported rolling sequence first, then canary clients through representative tiers while measuring server and client CPU/network, health-update latency, missed or duplicate events, and reconnect behavior; define rollback thresholds and complete the rollout before the peak.
critical_assumptions: The exact target 1.10 patch release supports `use_streaming_backend` for the deployed OS and architecture and is compatible with the current mixed client/server versions.
Every health subscriber can be moved without breaking older clients during a mixed-version period.

result.recommendation: Retain the JWKS, kid, cache, and overlap design, but do not automate monthly rotation until every validator instance—not merely every service—demonstrably uses the endpoint and refreshes on unknown kid. critical_assumptions: Every validator can use a kid-aware JWKS set, including gateways, SDKs, and custom implementations.

Validators refresh on unknown kid and can serve the newly published key within the stated cache TTL.
The readiness metric counts successful validation by JWKS for every active validator instance, rather than only aggregate token volume.
Key activation and retirement can be coordinated, with rollback available and the old private key retained for the required overlap window.
material_risks: A single remaining static-key validator can cause an outage when activation changes the signing kid, even if aggregate JWKS traffic is high.

The JWKS endpoint is authenticated, highly available, and protected against stale or partial key sets.
Validators can use the last successful JWKS response when the endpoint is temporarily unavailable.

Publish the new key, wait at least cache TTL plus maximum token lifetime before signing, then retain it until at least the last signing time plus token lifetime, maximum cache/stale-cache retention, and clock-skew margin; require an automatic rollback and tested outage behavior.

Automation or an incorrect clock variable removes a key too early or rotates again before the prior overlap completes.

falsification_probe.description: Scan the production service inventory and representative configurations/runtimes for one of: hardcoded public keys, no supported outbound JWKS access, missing kid handling, or no reliable per-instance validation-method telemetry.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: This would falsify the rollout premise if even one production validator cannot perform dynamic JWKS validation or cannot be individually identified; if none exist and canary cold/warm cache tests pass, it confirms the design is deployable.

result.recommendation: Keep the JWKS, `kid`, cache, unknown-`kid` refresh, and staged activation design, but add explicit preflight and monitoring requirements. Before each rotation, verify every validator has fetched the new key and enforce a configurable clock-skew/grace period; block removal of the old key until both token expiry and cache-expiry bounds are exceeded, with a manual emergency-compromise procedure.
critical_assumptions: Every validator can securely reach JWKS and will retry after startup or transient failures.
Validators enforce RS256 and select the key using the token's `kid` rather than accepting an arbitrary algorithm or key.
The 10-minute cache duration is an upper bound even during JWKS outages, and unknown-`kid` requests are rate-limited and fail closed.
A per-validator or fleet-wide metric can prove that every validator has successfully processed the new key.
The JWKS endpoint is highly available and its TLS/DNS/secrets-manager dependencies are monitored.

An incomplete fetch, clock skew, or unexpectedly long cache lifetime can cause removal of a key still needed for validation.

If `kid` or algorithm validation is not strictly enforced, key-confusion or cross-algorithm attacks could undermine the migration.
Monthly automation can overlap rotations or remove a key before a partial deployment has converged, especially with independently deployed services.

falsification_probe.description: Run a canary rotation in a non-production validator fleet: publish a new JWKS key, wait for the stated cache interval, issue a token with its `kid`, and test normal validation, JWKS outage behavior, unknown-`kid` refresh, and metrics/logs.

result.recommendation: Require an explicit validator inventory and deployment-level JWKS readiness signal, not only token counts, because inactive or low-traffic services may emit no validation metric and still hold only the baked public key. Make removal contingent on verified fleet-wide JWKS adoption and retain the old key for at least the signed-access-token lifetime plus clock skew; keep normal access-token overlap separate from an emergency-compromise procedure.
critical_assumptions: Every token validator can be inventoried and reports a deployment-level JWKS readiness state.
JWKS retrieval is authenticated or served over TLS with reliable availability, bounded timeouts, and negative-cache/rate-limit protection.
Validators can refresh keys without coordinated restarts and tolerate an unknown kid by retrying JWKS once.
Token issuance and validation clocks have bounded, monitored skew.

An unreachable or slow JWKS endpoint causes widespread validation failure unless cached keys remain usable.
Unknown-kid retry behavior creates a JWKS request amplification or denial-of-service vector.
Premature old-key removal invalidates still-valid access tokens.

falsification_probe.description: Compare the authoritative service/version inventory with deployment-level validation-method telemetry, including services with zero token traffic during the observation window.

result.recommendation: Retain the JWKS and staged-rotation design, but require an inventory-backed conformance test proving every validator supports `kid`, caches JWKS for the stated TTL, and retries unknown `kid` values. critical_assumptions: Every token-validating service, gateway, and relevant library supports JWKS, `kid`, and unknown-`kid` cache refresh.
Validators can either tolerate a 10-minute JWKS outage from cache or have a tested stale-cache fallback.
The longest validator disconnection or JWKS propagation delay is known and covered by the rollout procedure.
JWKS publication is consistent and reliable enough that signing begins only after validators have obtained the new key.
Refresh-token validation does not cryptographically depend on the rotated access-token signing key.

result.recommendation: Keep the JWKS-based overlap strategy, but make rollout and retirement explicitly fail-closed: inventory every validation path, require a successful JWKS fetch from each service, and alert on any fallback to baked-in keys or failures to refresh an unknown `kid`. A compromised or unavailable JWKS endpoint can prevent token validation or enable denial of service across essentially the entire service fleet.
Incorrect retirement timing, clock skew, or a key still used by an active signer can invalidate outstanding tokens and force users to reauthenticate.
Unknown-`kid` alerts and refetch behavior can be abused to generate sustained traffic and cache churn against the JWKS service.

falsification_probe.description: Run a rotation rehearsal in a representative environment: issue a token with a newly published `kid`, validate it through every service and validation path while the JWKS is served, then restart one validator and repeat; concurrently inspect telemetry for the validation method used by each request.

result.recommendation: Keep the JWKS and overlap-rotation approach, but define the overlap from the actual maximum remaining access-token lifetime plus clock skew, not merely the nominal TTL. Require configuration/runtime telemetry rather than token counts alone to prove every validator migrated, and add bounded stale-cache behavior, JWKS hardening, rate limiting, alerting, and a rehearsed rollback procedure before the first rotation.
critical_assumptions: Every access-token issuer uses the same centrally controlled key set and there are no additional or legacy signing paths.
Every validator can dynamically retrieve and cache multiple JWKS keys and treats an unknown kid as a refresh trigger.
The JWKS source is sufficiently available, authenticated, monitored, and protected against unauthorized key publication.
Removing a key after the access-token expiry and clock-skew window cannot invalidate opaque server-side refresh tokens or other artifacts.
Configuration or runtime telemetry can identify every validator, including low- or zero-traffic services, and distinguish JWKS from embedded-key validation.

An attacker could repeatedly present unknown kids, amplifying refetches into a JWKS denial-of-service or cache-poisoning event.
Incomplete migration telemetry could leave embedded-key validators active, causing inconsistent validation during rotation.
A publishing-path compromise could expose a forged public key and enable acceptance of attacker-signed tokens.
Monthly automation without explicit activation deadlines, ownership, and rollback criteria could leave multiple keys published indefinitely or delete one prematurely.

falsification_probe.description: Inventory every JWT-validation configuration and code path, recording key source, refresh behavior, deployment owner, and recent validation traffic; then run a test that rotates a canary key while forcing one representative validator to remain offline beyond the stated overlap.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The solution is falsified if any active validator cannot consume overlapping JWKS keys, any active path still uses a baked-in key, or the canary outage shows the overlap calculation is shorter than tokens actually remain accepted.

result.recommendation: Keep the JWKS and kid-based rotation direction, but make activation and retirement explicitly stateful and safe under partial outages. Before signing with a new key, require evidence that every validator supports unknown-kid refresh and can reach JWKS, and wait for the maximum observed cache TTL, token lifetime, clock skew, and deployment delay. Retain the old key for a defined safety margin rather than relying solely on a per-validator validation metric; separately document emergency compromise handling, which may conflict with the no-forced-logout constraint.
critical_assumptions: All validators support kid selection, multi-key verification, and an unknown-kid cache refresh.
The JWKS endpoint is highly available, authenticated or integrity-protected, and reachable from every validator environment.
Ten minutes is a true upper bound on validator cache refresh, including failures and retry behavior.
Metrics labeled as validation by JWKS also prove support for unknown kids rather than merely successful validation with a preloaded key.
A 15-minute access-token lifetime plus clock skew is the complete set of token-liveness constraints; refresh-token lifetime is irrelevant because those tokens are opaque.

A compromised JWKS publication path could distribute an attacker-controlled verification key, enabling forged access tokens.

Removing the old key based only on nominal token expiration could still break validators with unusually large clock skew, replay windows, or delayed processing.
Automation may continue publishing the old key after compromise, or may remove it too quickly during an incident, producing either continued exposure or mass logout.

Keep static-key configuration only as a temporary migration fallback with a hard removal deadline.

falsification_probe.description: Run a canary rotation using a new kid while forcing a representative validator to serve a stale 10-minute cache, then submit a token signed by the new key and inspect its unknown-kid behavior.
falsification_probe.expected_signal: The validator fetches the updated JWKS, selects the new kid, and accepts the token; failure to refresh, rejection, or acceptance only because the new key was preloaded falsifies the proposal's readiness criterion.

Ensure the pre-rotation verification covers idle and infrequently deployed validators through deployment/config inventory or an integration test, not traffic metrics alone, and retain the prior key until the access-token expiry window has elapsed after the final signing use.
critical_assumptions: All validators can be deployed with a JWKS client and have reliable access to the endpoint.
JWKS responses are authenticated, integrity-protected, and available with sufficient reliability for validator operation.
Validators correctly refresh on an unknown kid and tolerate overlapping active keys.
The signing key is not used to validate or revoke opaque refresh tokens.
A deployment inventory or equivalent control identifies validators that generate no validation traffic.

The stated 10-minute cache has a bounded, reliable refresh behavior; merely waiting 10 minutes does not force a fetch.
All validators enforce the 15-minute maximum access-token lifetime, including relevant clock-skew and `nbf`/`iat` checks.
JWKS publication and retrieval is highly available, cached through intermediaries safely, and protected against stale or inconsistent responses.
The old private key is disabled and destroyed through the secrets-management pipeline immediately after the new signer is activated.

A stale or unavailable JWKS endpoint can cause broad authentication outages or silently delay key adoption.

JWKS retrieval is authenticated or otherwise protected against key-substitution attacks.
No opaque refresh-token or other server-side token depends on the old signing key.

falsification_probe.description: Run a signed test access token with a newly generated kid through every known validator deployment and compare failures grouped by service and instance over a representative traffic period.

A validator that reports tokens by method can prove that its JWKS path is active, rather than merely reporting cached or fallback validation.

The old key is removed too early, invalidating remaining access tokens despite the nominal TTL calculation.
JWKS outage, blocking, rate limiting, or stale-cache behavior prevents unknown-kid recovery or cold starts.

Incorrect kid metadata, algorithm handling, or key publication ordering makes fetched keys unusable and triggers widespread validation failures.

falsification_probe.description: Publish a canary public key with a unique kid in JWKS but do not use it for normal traffic; run a test token through one validator per deployment configuration and, if possible, every active validator fleet segment, then compare JWKS fetch/refetch and validation metrics against the complete validator inventory.

result.recommendation: Keep the bit-reuse approach, but add an RLP runtime feature flag that defaults off, deploy and verify the new router build on all eight servers before clients set the bit, and canary enablement after mixed-version testing. The new router correctly rejects or safely handles RLP-marked orders before rollout completes.
Power Peg has no dormant side effects outside its supposedly unreachable routing branch.

Removing the old code path in the same release increases the consequences of any partial or failed deployment.
Client enablement occurring before router verification creates an immediate launch-day compatibility failure.

Removing the old Power Peg implementation cannot invalidate persisted state, hidden configuration, or downstream assumptions.
The router can distinguish an RLP order from an invalid or unexpected legacy order and fail closed.
